For simple $H_0: \theta_0$ versus simple $H_1: \theta_1$, the test that rejects when $L(\theta_0)/L(\theta_1) \le k$, with $k$ set to give size $\alpha$, is most powerful among tests of size at most $\alpha$.

A level-$\alpha$ test that is most powerful against every alternative in a composite $H_1$ at once; it exists for one-sided alternatives in families with a monotone likelihood ratio, but generally not for two-sided ones.
A family has a monotone likelihood ratio in a statistic $T$ if $L(\theta_1)/L(\theta_0)$ is an increasing function of $T$ whenever $\theta_1 > \theta_0$; one-parameter exponential families have it.
The test that rejects $H_0$ when $\Lambda = \sup_{\Omega_0}L(\theta)/\sup_{\Omega}L(\theta) = L(\hat\theta_0)/L(\hat\theta)$ is small.
Under regularity conditions and $H_0$, $-2\ln\Lambda$ is approximately $\chi^2_r$ for large samples, where $r = \dim\Omega - \dim\Omega_0$ is the number of parameters fixed by $H_0$.
The large-sample test of $p = p_0$ using $Z = (\hat p - p_0)/\sqrt{p_0(1 - p_0)/n}$, approximately $N(0,1)$ under $H_0$.
The large-sample test of $p_1 = p_2$ using $(\hat p_1 - \hat p_2)/\sqrt{\hat p(1 - \hat p)(1/n_1 + 1/n_2)}$ with the pooled proportion $\hat p$.
The estimate $\hat p = (X_1 + X_2)/(n_1 + n_2)$ of the common success probability under $H_0: p_1 = p_2$.
The count a cell would have on average if $H_0$ were true: $np_{i0}$ in a goodness-of-fit test, $R_iC_j/n$ in a two-way table.
The statistic $X^2 = \sum (O - E)^2/E$ over all cells, approximately chi-square under $H_0$ when expected counts are not too small.
A test of whether multinomial counts in $k$ categories follow specified probabilities; $X^2$ has approximately $k - 1 - m$ df, where $m$ parameters are estimated from the data.
A table of counts classifying each item by two categorical variables, with $r$ rows and $c$ columns.
A test of whether two categorical variables are independent, using $X^2$ with $E_{ij} = R_iC_j/n$ and $(r-1)(c-1)$ df.
A chi-square test of whether several separately sampled populations share the same distribution over categories; computed exactly like the test of independence.
The likelihood ratio statistic $G^2 = 2\sum O\ln(O/E)$ for counts; it equals $-2\ln\Lambda$ and is close to Pearson's $X^2$.
The model $Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1x_i + \varepsilon_i$ with fixed $x_i$ and independent errors $\varepsilon_i \sim N(0, \sigma^2)$.
Choosing $b_0, b_1$ to minimize $\sum(y_i - b_0 - b_1x_i)^2$; gives $b_1 = S_{xy}/S_{xx}$ and $b_0 = \bar y - b_1\bar x$.
The equations obtained by setting the partial derivatives of the sum of squared errors to zero; for a line they say $\sum e_i = 0$ and $\sum x_ie_i = 0$.
The difference $e_i = y_i - \hat y_i$ between an observed response and its fitted value.
Shorthand sums in regression: $S_{xx} = \sum(x_i - \bar x)^2$, $S_{xy} = \sum(x_i - \bar x)(y_i - \bar y)$, $S_{yy} = \sum(y_i - \bar y)^2$.
The unexplained variation: $\sum e_i^2$ in regression (on $n - 2$ df) or $\sum\sum(Y_{ij} - \bar Y_{i\cdot})^2$ in ANOVA (on $N - k$ df).
The total variation of the responses about their overall mean, $\sum(y - \bar y)^2$; it splits into an explained part and SSE.
The variation explained by the fitted line, $\text{SSR} = \sum(\hat y_i - \bar y)^2 = b_1^2S_{xx}$; $\text{SST} = \text{SSR} + \text{SSE}$.
The fraction of variation in $y$ explained by the regression, $r^2 = \text{SSR}/\text{SST} = 1 - \text{SSE}/\text{SST}$; for a line it is the squared correlation.

glossary.term: confidence interval for the mean response
aliases: confidence interval for a mean response
glossary.definition: An interval for $\beta_0 + \beta_1x_0$: $\hat y_0 \pm t_{\alpha/2,n-2}\,s\sqrt{1/n + (x_0 - \bar x)^2/S_{xx}}$.
An interval for a single new response at $x_0$: $\hat y_0 \pm t_{\alpha/2,n-2}\,s\sqrt{1 + 1/n + (x_0 - \bar x)^2/S_{xx}}$; wider than the mean-response interval because it includes the new error.

In a linear model with uncorrelated, equal-variance errors, the least squares estimators have the smallest variance among all linear unbiased estimators (they are BLUE: best linear unbiased estimators).
A method that tests equality of several means by comparing variation between group means with variation within groups, using $F = \text{MSTr}/\text{MSE}$.
The between-group variation $\text{SSTr} = \sum n_i(\bar Y_{i\cdot} - \bar Y_{\cdot\cdot})^2$, on $k - 1$ df.
A sum of squares divided by its degrees of freedom, such as $\text{MSTr} = \text{SSTr}/(k-1)$ and the error mean square $\text{SSE}/(N-k)$, which estimates $\sigma^2$.
A table listing, for each source of variation (treatments, error, total), its df, sum of squares, mean square, and the $F$ statistic with its p-value.
The probability of making at least one Type I error among a whole family of tests or comparisons.
Running each of $m$ comparisons at level $\alpha/m$; by the union bound the familywise error rate is at most $\alpha$.

A multiple comparison procedure for all pairwise differences of means, based on the distribution of the largest standardized difference; it controls the familywise error rate exactly for equal group sizes.
Follow-up comparisons among group means after ANOVA, done with a method (Bonferroni, Tukey) that controls the familywise error rate.
A test whose null distribution does not depend on the population's distribution (beyond continuity or symmetry), typically because it uses only signs or ranks.
A test of a median (or median difference) using the number of positive observations, which is $\text{Bin}(n, 1/2)$ under $H_0$; zeros are dropped.

A one-sample or paired test that ranks $\lvert D_i\rvert$ and sums the ranks of positive differences, $W^+$; under $H_0$ (symmetry about 0) $E(W^+) = n(n+1)/4$ and $\operatorname{Var}(W^+) = n(n+1)(2n+1)/24$.
A two-sample test using $W$, the sum of the first sample's ranks in the combined sample; under $H_0$ $E(W) = m(N+1)/2$ and $\operatorname{Var}(W) = mn(N+1)/12$.
The statistic $U = W - m(m+1)/2$, the number of pairs with $X_i > Y_j$; equivalent to the Wilcoxon rank-sum test, and $U/(mn)$ estimates $P(X > Y)$.
The rank-based alternative to one-way ANOVA: rank all observations together and compare group average ranks; approximately $\chi^2_{k-1}$ under $H_0$.

A test that computes a statistic for every relabeling of the data (or a random sample of relabelings) that is equally likely under $H_0$, and reports the fraction at least as extreme as the observed value.
The limiting ratio of sample sizes two tests need for equal power; Wilcoxon versus $t$ is $3/\pi \approx 0.955$ for normal data, and the sign test versus $t$ is $2/\pi \approx 0.64$.

references.title: Joint distributions, limit theorems and estimation
references.body:
## Joint distributions

| Quantity | Discrete | Continuous |
|---|---|---|
| Probability of an event $A$ | $\sum_{(x,y) \in A} p(x, y)$ | $\iint_A f(x, y)\,dA$ |
| Marginal of $X$ | $p_X(x) = \sum_y p(x, y)$ | $f_X(x) = \int f(x, y)\,dy$ |
| Conditional of $Y$ given $X = x$ | $p(x, y)/p_X(x)$ | $f(x, y)/f_X(x)$ |
| Independence | $p(x, y) = p_X(x)p_Y(y)$ | $f(x, y) = f_X(x)f_Y(y)$ (rectangular support) |
| $E[g(X, Y)]$ | $\sum\sum g\,p$ | $\iint g\,f\,dA$ |

## Expectation, covariance, conditioning

| Identity | Formula |
|---|---|
| Covariance | $\operatorname{Cov}(X, Y) = E[XY] - E[X]E[Y]$ |
| Linear functions | $\operatorname{Cov}(aX + b, cY + d) = ac\operatorname{Cov}(X, Y)$ |
| Correlation | $\rho = \operatorname{Cov}(X, Y)/(\sigma_X\sigma_Y)$, $-1 \le \rho \le 1$ |
| Variance of a combination | $\operatorname{Var}(aX + bY) = a^2\operatorname{Var}X + b^2\operatorname{Var}Y + 2ab\operatorname{Cov}(X, Y)$ |
| iid sample mean | $E[\bar X] = \mu$, $\operatorname{Var}(\bar X) = \sigma^2/n$ |
| Total expectation | $E[Y] = E[E[Y \mid X]]$ |
| Total variance | $\operatorname{Var}(Y) = E[\operatorname{Var}(Y \mid X)] + \operatorname{Var}(E[Y \mid X])$ |
| Random sum $T = \sum_{i=1}^N X_i$ | $E[T] = \mu E[N]$, $\operatorname{Var}(T) = \sigma^2E[N] + \mu^2\operatorname{Var}(N)$ |

## Sums of independent random variables

| Rule | Result |
|---|---|
| Discrete convolution | $P(X + Y = z) = \sum_k p_X(k)p_Y(z - k)$ |
| Continuous convolution | $f_{X+Y}(z) = \int f_X(x)f_Y(z - x)\,dx$ |
| MGFs | $M_{X+Y}(t) = M_X(t)M_Y(t)$ |
| Poisson | $\text{Pois}(\lambda_1) + \text{Pois}(\lambda_2) = \text{Pois}(\lambda_1 + \lambda_2)$ |
| Binomial (same $p$) | $\text{Bin}(n_1, p) + \text{Bin}(n_2, p) = \text{Bin}(n_1 + n_2, p)$ |
| Normal | $aX + bY \sim N(a\mu_1 + b\mu_2,\ a^2\sigma_1^2 + b^2\sigma_2^2)$ |
| Gamma (shape $\alpha_i$, same scale $\theta$) | $\text{Gamma}(\alpha_1, \theta) + \text{Gamma}(\alpha_2, \theta) = \text{Gamma}(\alpha_1 + \alpha_2, \theta)$; $n$ iid exponentials with mean $\theta$ sum to Gamma($n, \theta$) |

## Bivariate normal and order statistics

| Fact | Formula |
|---|---|
| Conditional mean | $E[Y \mid X = x] = \mu_Y + \rho\dfrac{\sigma_Y}{\sigma_X}(x - \mu_X)$ |
| Conditional variance | $\operatorname{Var}(Y \mid X = x) = \sigma_Y^2(1 - \rho^2)$ |
| $\rho = 0$ | independent (bivariate normal only) |
| Maximum of $n$ iid | $F_{\max}(x) = F(x)^n$, $f_{\max} = nF^{n-1}f$ |
| Minimum of $n$ iid | $F_{\min}(x) = 1 - (1 - F(x))^n$, $f_{\min} = n(1 - F)^{n-1}f$ |
| $k$th order statistic | $f_{(k)}(x) = \dfrac{n!}{(k-1)!(n-k)!}F^{k-1}(1 - F)^{n-k}f$ |
| Uniform(0, 1) | $E[X_{(k)}] = k/(n + 1)$ |

## Limit theorems

| Result | Statement |
|---|---|
| Markov | $X \ge 0$: $P(X \ge a) \le E[X]/a$ |
| Chebyshev | $P(\lvert X - \mu\rvert \ge k\sigma) \le 1/k^2$; $P(\lvert X - \mu\rvert \ge \varepsilon) \le \sigma^2/\varepsilon^2$ |
| Weak law of large numbers | $P(\lvert\bar X_n - \mu\rvert \ge \varepsilon) \le \dfrac{\sigma^2}{n\varepsilon^2} \to 0$ |
| Central Limit Theorem | $\dfrac{\bar X_n - \mu}{\sigma/\sqrt n} \xrightarrow{d} N(0, 1)$; $S_n \approx N(n\mu, n\sigma^2)$ |
| Binomial approximation | $\text{Bin}(n, p) \approx N(np, np(1-p))$, continuity correction $\pm 0.5$ |

## Sampling distributions (normal population)

| Statistic | Distribution |
|---|---|
| $\bar X$ | $N(\mu, \sigma^2/n)$ |
| $(n-1)S^2/\sigma^2$ | $\chi^2_{n-1}$, independent of $\bar X$ |
| $(\bar X - \mu)/(S/\sqrt n)$ | $t_{n-1}$ |
| $(S_1^2/\sigma_1^2)/(S_2^2/\sigma_2^2)$ | $F_{n_1 - 1,\,n_2 - 1}$ |
| $\chi^2_\nu$ | mean $\nu$, variance $2\nu$; Gamma(shape $\nu/2$, scale 2) |
| $Z/\sqrt{V/\nu}$ | $t_\nu$; $T^2 \sim F_{1,\nu}$ |

## Estimators

| Concept | Formula |
|---|---|
| Bias | $E[\hat\theta] - \theta$ |
| Mean squared error | $\operatorname{MSE} = \operatorname{Var}(\hat\theta) + \operatorname{Bias}^2$ |
| Unbiased variance | $S^2 = \frac{1}{n-1}\sum(X_i - \bar X)^2$; $\hat\sigma^2 = \frac1n\sum(X_i - \bar X)^2$ has bias $-\sigma^2/n$ |
| Fisher information | $I(\theta) = -E\big[\partial_\theta^2\ln f(X; \theta)\big]$ |
| Cramér–Rao bound | $\operatorname{Var}(\hat\theta) \ge 1/(nI(\theta))$ (unbiased, regular family) |
| Large-sample MLE | $\hat\theta \approx N(\theta, 1/(nI(\theta)))$ |

| Model | MoM | MLE | $I(\theta)$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| Bernoulli($p$) | $\bar x$ | $\bar x$ | $1/(p(1-p))$ |
| Poisson($\lambda$) | $\bar x$ | $\bar x$ | $1/\lambda$ |
| Exponential (rate $\lambda$) | $1/\bar x$ | $1/\bar x$ | $1/\lambda^2$ |
| Geometric($p$), $x \ge 1$ | $1/\bar x$ | $1/\bar x$ | $1/(p^2(1-p))$ |
| $N(\mu, \sigma^2)$ | $\bar x$, $\frac1n\sum(x_i - \bar x)^2$ | same | $1/\sigma^2$ for $\mu$ |
| Uniform$(0, \theta)$ | $2\bar x$ | $\max x_i$ | (not regular) |

## Confidence intervals

| Parameter | Pivot | Interval |
|---|---|---|
| $\mu$, $\sigma$ known | $\dfrac{\bar X - \mu}{\sigma/\sqrt n} \sim N(0, 1)$ | $\bar x \pm z_{\alpha/2}\,\sigma/\sqrt n$ |
| $\mu$, $\sigma$ unknown | $\dfrac{\bar X - \mu}{S/\sqrt n} \sim t_{n-1}$ | $\bar x \pm t_{\alpha/2,n-1}\,s/\sqrt n$ |
| $\sigma^2$ | $\dfrac{(n-1)S^2}{\sigma^2} \sim \chi^2_{n-1}$ | $\left[\dfrac{(n-1)s^2}{\chi^2_U},\ \dfrac{(n-1)s^2}{\chi^2_L}\right]$ |
| $p$ (large $n$) | $\dfrac{\hat p - p}{\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}} \approx N(0, 1)$ | $\hat p \pm z_{\alpha/2}\sqrt{\hat p(1-\hat p)/n}$ |
| $\mu_1 - \mu_2$, $\sigma$'s known | normal | $(\bar x_1 - \bar x_2) \pm z_{\alpha/2}\sqrt{\sigma_1^2/n_1 + \sigma_2^2/n_2}$ |
| $\mu_1 - \mu_2$, equal unknown $\sigma$ | $t_{n_1+n_2-2}$ | $(\bar x_1 - \bar x_2) \pm t_{\alpha/2}\,s_p\sqrt{1/n_1 + 1/n_2}$ |
| $p_1 - p_2$ (large $n$) | normal | $(\hat p_1 - \hat p_2) \pm z_{\alpha/2}\sqrt{\frac{\hat p_1(1-\hat p_1)}{n_1} + \frac{\hat p_2(1-\hat p_2)}{n_2}}$ |
| Exponential rate $\lambda$ | $2\lambda\sum X_i \sim \chi^2_{2n}$ | $\left[\dfrac{\chi^2_L}{2\sum x_i},\ \dfrac{\chi^2_U}{2\sum x_i}\right]$ |

Pooled variance: $s_p^2 = \dfrac{(n_1 - 1)s_1^2 + (n_2 - 1)s_2^2}{n_1 + n_2 - 2}$. Sample size for margin $E$: $n = (z_{\alpha/2}\sigma/E)^2$, rounded up.
$\chi^2_L$ and $\chi^2_U$ are the $\alpha/2$ and $1 - \alpha/2$ quantiles. Common $z_{\alpha/2}$: 1.645 (90%), 1.960 (95%), 2.576 (99%).

## Bayesian conjugate updates

| Data | Prior | Posterior | Posterior mean |
|---|---|---|---|
| $x$ successes in $n$ trials | Beta$(a, b)$ | Beta$(a + x,\ b + n - x)$ | $\dfrac{a + x}{a + b + n}$ |
| $n$ Poisson counts | Gamma$(\alpha, \beta)$ (shape $\alpha$, rate $\beta$) | Gamma$(\alpha + \sum x_i,\ \beta + n)$ | $\dfrac{\alpha + \sum x_i}{\beta + n}$ |
| $n$ readings $N(\theta, \sigma^2)$, $\sigma$ known | $N(\mu_0, \tau_0^2)$ | $N(\mu_n, \tau_n^2)$, $\dfrac{1}{\tau_n^2} = \dfrac{1}{\tau_0^2} + \dfrac{n}{\sigma^2}$ | $\mu_n = \tau_n^2\left(\dfrac{\mu_0}{\tau_0^2} + \dfrac{n\bar x}{\sigma^2}\right)$ |

Beta$(\alpha, \beta)$ mode (MAP): $(\alpha - 1)/(\alpha + \beta - 2)$. Equal-tailed credible interval: the $\alpha/2$ and $1 - \alpha/2$ posterior quantiles.

references.title: Probability rules and distributions
references.body:
## Probability rules

| Rule | Formula |
|---|---|
| Complement | $P(A^c) = 1 - P(A)$ |
| Addition | $P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)$ |
| Inclusion–exclusion (3 events) | $\sum P(A_i) - \sum_{i<j} P(A_i \cap A_j) + P(A_1 \cap A_2 \cap A_3)$ |
| Union bound | $P(\bigcup A_i) \le \sum P(A_i)$ |
| Bonferroni | $P(A \cap B) \ge P(A) + P(B) - 1$ |
| De Morgan | $(A \cup B)^c = A^c \cap B^c$, $(A \cap B)^c = A^c \cup B^c$ |
| Conditional probability | $P(A \mid B) = P(A \cap B)/P(B)$ |
| Multiplication / chain rule | $P(A \cap B \cap C) = P(A)P(B \mid A)P(C \mid A \cap B)$ |
| Total probability | $P(A) = \sum_i P(B_i)P(A \mid B_i)$ for a partition $B_1, \ldots, B_k$ |
| Bayes | $P(B_j \mid A) = \dfrac{P(B_j)P(A \mid B_j)}{\sum_i P(B_i)P(A \mid B_i)}$ |
| Odds form of Bayes | posterior odds = prior odds × $\dfrac{P(A \mid B)}{P(A \mid B^c)}$ |
| Independence | $P(A \cap B) = P(A)P(B)$ |
| At least one success in $n$ trials | $1 - (1 - p)^n$ |
| Series / parallel reliability | $\prod p_i$ / $1 - \prod (1 - p_i)$ |

## Counting

| Selection of $r$ from $n$ | Count |
|---|---|
| Ordered, no repeats | $\dfrac{n!}{(n-r)!}$ |
| Ordered, repeats allowed | $n^r$ |
| Unordered, no repeats | $\dbinom{n}{r} = \dfrac{n!}{r!\,(n-r)!}$ |
| Split $n$ into labeled groups $n_1, \ldots, n_k$ | $\dfrac{n!}{n_1!\cdots n_k!}$ |
| Birthday: no match among $n$ | $\prod_{i=0}^{n-1}(1 - i/365)$ |
| Matching: at least one match | $\sum_{k=1}^{n} (-1)^{k+1}/k! \approx 1 - e^{-1}$ |

## Expectation and variance

| Quantity | Discrete | Continuous |
|---|---|---|
| Total probability | $\sum p(x) = 1$ | $\int f(x)\,dx = 1$ |
| cdf | $F(x) = \sum_{t \le x} p(t)$ | $F(x) = \int_{-\infty}^x f(t)\,dt$, $F' = f$ |
| Mean | $\sum x\,p(x)$ | $\int x f(x)\,dx$ |
| LOTUS | $E[g(X)] = \sum g(x)p(x)$ | $E[g(X)] = \int g(x) f(x)\,dx$ |
| Tail formula ($X \ge 0$) | $E(X) = \sum_{k \ge 0} P(X > k)$ (integer values) | $E(X) = \int_0^\infty P(X > x)\,dx$ |

- $\operatorname{Var}(X) = E(X^2) - [E(X)]^2$; $E(aX + b) = aE(X) + b$; $\operatorname{Var}(aX + b) = a^2\operatorname{Var}(X)$.
- MGF $M_X(t) = E(e^{tX})$: $E(X^k) = M^{(k)}(0)$; $M_{aX+b}(t) = e^{bt}M_X(at)$; $M_{X+Y} = M_XM_Y$ if independent.
- With $R(t) = \ln M_X(t)$: $\mu = R'(0)$, $\sigma^2 = R''(0)$.

## Discrete distributions ($q = 1 - p$)

| Distribution | pmf | Mean | Variance | MGF |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bernoulli$(p)$ | $p^x q^{1-x}$, $x = 0, 1$ | $p$ | $pq$ | $q + pe^t$ |
| Binomial$(n, p)$ | $\binom{n}{k}p^kq^{n-k}$, $k = 0..n$ | $np$ | $npq$ | $(q + pe^t)^n$ |
| Hypergeometric$(N, K, n)$ | $\dfrac{\binom{K}{k}\binom{N-K}{n-k}}{\binom{N}{n}}$ | $n\dfrac{K}{N}$ | $n\dfrac{K}{N}\left(1 - \dfrac{K}{N}\right)\dfrac{N-n}{N-1}$ | — |
| Geometric$(p)$, trials | $q^{k-1}p$, $k \ge 1$ | $\dfrac1p$ | $\dfrac{q}{p^2}$ | $\dfrac{pe^t}{1 - qe^t}$ |
| Negative binomial$(r, p)$ | $\binom{k-1}{r-1}p^rq^{k-r}$, $k \ge r$ | $\dfrac{r}{p}$ | $\dfrac{rq}{p^2}$ | $\left(\dfrac{pe^t}{1 - qe^t}\right)^r$ |
| Poisson$(\lambda)$ | $e^{-\lambda}\dfrac{\lambda^k}{k!}$, $k \ge 0$ | $\lambda$ | $\lambda$ | $e^{\lambda(e^t - 1)}$ |

Geometric tail: $P(X > k) = q^k$. Poisson process with rate $\lambda$: count in time $t$ is Poisson$(\lambda t)$.

## Continuous distributions

| Distribution | pdf | Mean | Variance | MGF |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Uniform$(a, b)$ | $\dfrac{1}{b - a}$, $a \le x \le b$ | $\dfrac{a + b}{2}$ | $\dfrac{(b - a)^2}{12}$ | $\dfrac{e^{tb} - e^{ta}}{t(b - a)}$ |
| Exponential$(\lambda)$ | $\lambda e^{-\lambda x}$, $x \ge 0$ | $\dfrac1\lambda$ | $\dfrac{1}{\lambda^2}$ | $\dfrac{\lambda}{\lambda - t}$, $t < \lambda$ |
| Normal$(\mu, \sigma^2)$ | $\dfrac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-(x - \mu)^2/(2\sigma^2)}$ | $\mu$ | $\sigma^2$ | $e^{\mu t + \sigma^2t^2/2}$ |
| Gamma$(\alpha, \theta)$, scale $\theta$ | $\dfrac{x^{\alpha - 1}e^{-x/\theta}}{\Gamma(\alpha)\theta^\alpha}$, $x > 0$ | $\alpha\theta$ | $\alpha\theta^2$ | $(1 - \theta t)^{-\alpha}$, $t < 1/\theta$ |
| Chi-square$(\nu)$ | Gamma$(\nu/2, 2)$ | $\nu$ | $2\nu$ | $(1 - 2t)^{-\nu/2}$ |
| Beta$(a, b)$ | $\dfrac{x^{a-1}(1 - x)^{b-1}}{B(a, b)}$, $0 < x < 1$ | $\dfrac{a}{a + b}$ | $\dfrac{ab}{(a + b)^2(a + b + 1)}$ | — |

- Exponential: $P(X > x) = e^{-\lambda x}$, median $\ln 2/\lambda$, memoryless.
- Normal: $Z = (X - \mu)/\sigma$; $x_p = \mu + \sigma z_p$; $z_{0.90} = 1.2816$, $z_{0.95} = 1.6449$, $z_{0.975} = 1.9600$, $z_{0.99} = 2.3263$.
- Binomial ≈ Normal$(np, npq)$ when $np, nq \ge 10$; continuity correction $P(X \le k) \approx \Phi\left(\frac{k + 0.5 - np}{\sqrt{npq}}\right)$.
- Gamma function: $\Gamma(\alpha + 1) = \alpha\Gamma(\alpha)$, $\Gamma(n) = (n-1)!$, $\Gamma(\tfrac12) = \sqrt\pi$; $\int_0^\infty x^{\alpha-1}e^{-x/\theta}dx = \Gamma(\alpha)\theta^\alpha$.
- Beta function: $B(a, b) = \Gamma(a)\Gamma(b)/\Gamma(a + b)$.
- Time of the $k$-th event of a rate-$\lambda$ Poisson process: Gamma$(k, 1/\lambda)$, with $P(T_k > t) = P(\text{Poisson}(\lambda t) \le k - 1)$.

## Functions of a random variable

| Method | Formula |
|---|---|
| Discrete | $p_Y(y) = \sum_{g(x) = y} p_X(x)$ |
| cdf method | $F_Y(y) = P(g(X) \le y)$, then $f_Y = F_Y'$ |
| Monotone $g$ | $f_Y(y) = f_X(g^{-1}(y))\left\lvert \dfrac{d}{dy}g^{-1}(y)\right\rvert$ |
| Linear $Y = aX + b$ | $f_Y(y) = \dfrac{1}{\lvert a \rvert}f_X\left(\dfrac{y - b}{a}\right)$ |
| Probability integral transform | $F(X) \sim$ Uniform$(0, 1)$; $F^{-1}(U)$ has cdf $F$ |

references.title: Hypothesis tests, regression and ANOVA
references.body:
## Framework

| Quantity | Definition |
|---|---|
| Power function | $\pi(\theta) = P_\theta(\text{reject } H_0)$ |
| Size | $\alpha = \sup_{\theta \in \Omega_0}\pi(\theta)$ |
| Type II error at $\theta \in \Omega_1$ | $\beta(\theta) = 1 - \pi(\theta)$ |
| p-value (upper-tailed) | $P_{\theta_0}(T \ge t_{\text{obs}})$; two-sided: double the smaller tail (symmetric null) |
| Sample size, one-sided $z$ | $n \ge \big((z_\alpha + z_\beta)\sigma/\delta\big)^2$ (two-sided: $z_{\alpha/2}$) |

Rejection regions: $H_1: \theta > \theta_0$ → upper tail; $\theta < \theta_0$ → lower tail; $\theta \ne \theta_0$ → both tails, $\alpha/2$ each.

## Tests for normal samples

| $H_0$ | Statistic | Null distribution |
|---|---|---|
| $\mu = \mu_0$, $\sigma$ known | $Z = \dfrac{\bar X - \mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt n}$ | $N(0, 1)$ |
| $\mu = \mu_0$ | $T = \dfrac{\bar X - \mu_0}{S/\sqrt n}$ | $t_{n-1}$ |
| $\mu_D = \Delta_0$ (paired) | $T = \dfrac{\bar D - \Delta_0}{S_D/\sqrt n}$ | $t_{n-1}$ |
| $\mu_1 - \mu_2 = \Delta_0$, $\sigma_1 = \sigma_2$ | $T = \dfrac{\bar X - \bar Y - \Delta_0}{S_p\sqrt{1/m + 1/n}}$ | $t_{m+n-2}$ |
| $\mu_1 - \mu_2 = \Delta_0$ (Welch) | $T = \dfrac{\bar X - \bar Y - \Delta_0}{\sqrt{S_1^2/m + S_2^2/n}}$ | $\approx t_\nu$ |
| $\sigma^2 = \sigma_0^2$ | $\chi^2 = (n-1)S^2/\sigma_0^2$ | $\chi^2_{n-1}$ |
| $\sigma_1^2 = \sigma_2^2$ | $F = S_1^2/S_2^2$ | $F_{m-1,\,n-1}$ |

$$S_p^2 = \frac{(m-1)S_1^2 + (n-1)S_2^2}{m+n-2}, \qquad \nu = \frac{(S_1^2/m + S_2^2/n)^2}{\dfrac{(S_1^2/m)^2}{m-1} + \dfrac{(S_2^2/n)^2}{n-1}}, \qquad F_{1-\alpha,\,a,\,b} = \frac{1}{F_{\alpha,\,b,\,a}}.$$

## Most powerful and likelihood ratio tests

| Result | Statement |
|---|---|
| Neyman–Pearson | Simple vs simple: reject when $L(\theta_0)/L(\theta_1) \le k$, size $\alpha$ → most powerful |
| UMP | Exists for one-sided $H_1$ with a monotone likelihood ratio; usually not for two-sided |
| LRT | $\Lambda = L(\hat\theta_0)/L(\hat\theta)$; reject for small $\Lambda$ |
| Wilks | $-2\ln\Lambda \approx \chi^2_r$, $r = \dim\Omega - \dim\Omega_0$ |
| Exponential sums | $2\lambda\sum X_i \sim \chi^2_{2n}$ |
| Poisson | $-2\ln\Lambda = 2n[\bar x\ln(\bar x/\lambda_0) - (\bar x - \lambda_0)]$ |
| Binomial | $-2\ln\Lambda = 2[x\ln\frac{x}{np_0} + (n-x)\ln\frac{n-x}{n(1-p_0)}]$ |

## Proportions and counts

| Test | Statistic | Reference |
|---|---|---|
| One proportion | $Z = \dfrac{\hat p - p_0}{\sqrt{p_0(1-p_0)/n}}$ | $N(0,1)$ |
| Two proportions | $Z = \dfrac{\hat p_1 - \hat p_2}{\sqrt{\hat p(1-\hat p)(1/n_1 + 1/n_2)}}$, $\hat p = \dfrac{X_1 + X_2}{n_1 + n_2}$ | $N(0,1)$ |
| Goodness of fit | $X^2 = \sum(O_i - E_i)^2/E_i$, $E_i = np_{i0}$ | $\chi^2_{k-1-m}$ |
| Independence / homogeneity | $X^2 = \sum(O_{ij} - E_{ij})^2/E_{ij}$, $E_{ij} = R_iC_j/n$ | $\chi^2_{(r-1)(c-1)}$ |
| Likelihood ratio version | $G^2 = 2\sum O\ln(O/E)$ | same df |

Use the chi-square approximations when all expected counts are at least about 5.

## Simple linear regression

$S_{xx} = \sum(x_i - \bar x)^2$, $S_{xy} = \sum(x_i - \bar x)(y_i - \bar y)$, $S_{yy} = \sum(y_i - \bar y)^2$.

| Quantity | Formula |
|---|---|
| Slope, intercept | $b_1 = S_{xy}/S_{xx}$, $b_0 = \bar y - b_1\bar x$ |
| SSE, $s^2$ | $\text{SSE} = S_{yy} - b_1S_{xy}$, $s^2 = \text{SSE}/(n-2)$ |
| Variances | $\operatorname{Var}(b_1) = \sigma^2/S_{xx}$, $\operatorname{Var}(b_0) = \sigma^2(1/n + \bar x^2/S_{xx})$ |
| Slope test / interval | $t = \dfrac{b_1 - \beta_{10}}{s/\sqrt{S_{xx}}}$ on $n - 2$ df; $b_1 \pm t_{\alpha/2,n-2}\,s/\sqrt{S_{xx}}$ |
| Mean response at $x_0$ | $\hat y_0 \pm t_{\alpha/2,n-2}\,s\sqrt{1/n + (x_0 - \bar x)^2/S_{xx}}$ |
| New observation at $x_0$ | $\hat y_0 \pm t_{\alpha/2,n-2}\,s\sqrt{1 + 1/n + (x_0 - \bar x)^2/S_{xx}}$ |
| Decomposition | $\text{SST} = \text{SSR} + \text{SSE}$, $r^2 = \text{SSR}/\text{SST}$, $F = \text{SSR}/s^2 = t^2$ |

## One-way ANOVA

| Source | df | SS | MS | F |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Treatments | $k - 1$ | $\sum n_i(\bar y_{i\cdot} - \bar y_{\cdot\cdot})^2$ | $\text{SSTr}/(k-1)$ | $\text{MSTr}/\text{MSE}$ |
| Error | $N - k$ | $\sum(n_i - 1)s_i^2$ | $\text{SSE}/(N-k)$ | |
| Total | $N - 1$ | $\sum\sum(y_{ij} - \bar y_{\cdot\cdot})^2$ | | |

Under $H_0$: $F \sim F_{k-1,\,N-k}$; reject for large $F$. Bonferroni pairwise:
$\bar y_i - \bar y_j \pm t_{\alpha/(2m),\,N-k}\sqrt{\text{MSE}(1/n_i + 1/n_j)}$ for $m$ comparisons.

## Nonparametric tests

| Test | Statistic | Null mean | Null variance |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sign | $B$ = number of positive differences (zeros dropped) | $n/2$ | $n/4$ (exactly $\text{Bin}(n, 1/2)$) |
| Signed-rank | $W^+$ = sum of ranks of $\lvert D_i\rvert$ with $D_i > 0$ | $n(n+1)/4$ | $n(n+1)(2n+1)/24$ |
| Rank-sum | $W$ = sum of sample-1 ranks in the combined sample | $m(N+1)/2$ | $mn(N+1)/12$ |
| Mann–Whitney | $U = W - m(m+1)/2$ | $mn/2$ | $mn(N+1)/12$ |

Large samples: $z = (\text{statistic} - \text{mean})/\sqrt{\text{variance}}$. Rank-based alternative to ANOVA: Kruskal–Wallis ($\approx \chi^2_{k-1}$).

drills.title: Addition rule and Venn regions
drills.prompt:
For events $A$ and $B$, $P(A) = {pa}$, $P(B) = {pb}$ and $P(A \cap B) = {pab}$. Find
$P(A \cup B)$, $P(A \cap B^c)$ (A but not B), and the probability that neither occurs.
drills.solution:
Addition rule: $P(A \cup B) = {pa} + {pb} - {pab} =$ **{uni:num2}**.
$A$ splits into $A \cap B$ and $A \cap B^c$, so $P(A \cap B^c) = {pa} - {pab} =$ **{aonly:num2}**.
By De Morgan, neither $= (A \cup B)^c$: $1 - {uni:num2} =$ **{nei:num2}**.

drills.title: Inclusion–exclusion with divisibility
drills.prompt:
An integer is chosen uniformly at random from $1, 2, \ldots, {nn:dp0}$. How many of these integers
are divisible by at least one of {a}, {b} and {c}, and what is the probability that the
chosen integer is (4 decimals)?
drills.solution:
The three numbers are pairwise relatively prime, so "divisible by both {a} and {b}" means
divisible by {ab}, and so on. Count multiples with $\lfloor {nn:dp0}/d \rfloor$:

- singles: ${na:dp0} + {nb:dp0} + {nc:dp0} = {singles:dp0}$;
- pairs (multiples of {ab}, {ac}, {bc}): ${nab} + {nac} + {nbc} = {pairs:dp0}$;
- triple (multiples of {abc}): ${nabc}$.

Inclusion–exclusion: ${singles:dp0} - {pairs:dp0} + {nabc} =$ **{cnt:dp0}**, so the probability is
${cnt:dp0}/{nn:dp0} =$ **{pr:num4}**.

drills.title: Probability of a committee's makeup
drills.prompt:
A team of {r} is chosen at random from {m} engineers and {w} analysts. What is the
probability that the team contains exactly {k} engineers? (4 decimals, or an exact fraction)
drills.solution:
All $\binom{{tot}}{{r}} = {cs:dp0}$ teams are equally likely. Favorable teams choose {k} of the
{m} engineers and {rk} of the {w} analysts: $\binom{{m}}{{k}}\binom{{w}}{{rk}} = {c1:dp0} \times {c2:dp0} = {fav:dp0}$.
So $P = {fav:dp0}/{cs:dp0} \approx$ **{pr:num4}**.

drills.title: Arrangements with identical objects
drills.prompt:
A row of {n} flags is made from {r} red, {bl} blue and {gr} green flags (identical within each
color), arranged in random order. How many distinct displays are there, and what is the
probability that all {r} red flags are next to each other? (Exact fraction.)
drills.solution:
Displays: $\dfrac{{n}!}{{r}!\,{bl}!\,{gr}!} =$ **{tot:dp0}**.
Glue the reds into one block; now arrange {m} items (the block, {bl} blue, {gr} green):
$\dfrac{{m}!}{{bl}!\,{gr}!} = {adj:dp0}$. So $P = \dfrac{{adj:dp0}}{{tot:dp0}} =$ **{pr:frac}**.

drills.title: The birthday problem
drills.prompt:
Each of {n} people independently picks one of {d} equally likely codes. What is the
probability that at least two people pick the same code? (4 decimals)
drills.solution:
Complement: all codes different. Ordered choices with no repeat over all ordered choices:
$$P(\text{no match}) = \frac{{d} \cdot {dm1} \cdots {last}}{{d}^{{n}}} = \prod_{i=0}^{{nm}}\left(1 - \frac{i}{{d}}\right) \approx {p0:num4}.$$
So $P(\text{at least one match}) \approx$ **{pm:num4}**.

drills.title: Draws without replacement
drills.prompt:
A bin has {nn} parts, of which {dd} are defective. Parts are drawn one at a time without
replacement. Find (a) the probability that the first 3 parts drawn are all defective and
(b) the probability that the second part drawn is defective. Give 4 significant figures or
exact fractions.
drills.solution:
(a) Chain rule: multiply the chance of a defective at each draw given the earlier ones,
$\dfrac{{dd}}{{nn}}\cdot\dfrac{{d1}}{{n1}}\cdot\dfrac{{d2}}{{n2}} \approx$ **{pall:sig4}**.

(b) Total probability over the first draw:
$\dfrac{{dd}}{{nn}}\cdot\dfrac{{d1}}{{n1}} + \dfrac{{g}}{{nn}}\cdot\dfrac{{dd}}{{n1}} = \dfrac{{dd}({d1} + {g})}{{nn}\cdot{n1}} = \dfrac{{dd}}{{nn}} \approx$ **{p2:sig4}**.
Unconditionally, every draw has the original proportion of defectives.

drills.title: Total probability and Bayes with three sources
drills.prompt:
Suppliers A, B and C provide {s1}%, {s2}% and {s3}% of a depot's brake pads. Their defect
rates are {r1}%, {r2}% and {r3}%. Find the probability that a randomly chosen pad is defective
(5 decimals), and the probability that a defective pad came from supplier {j} (4 decimals).
drills.solution:
Paths ending in "defective": A: ${t1:dp5}$, B: ${t2:dp5}$, C: ${t3:dp5}$
(share times defect rate). Total probability: $P(\text{defective}) =$ **{pd:dp5}**.
Bayes: the path through {j} over the total, ${tj:dp5}/{pd:dp5} \approx$ **{post:num4}**.

drills.title: Positive predictive value of a test
drills.prompt:
A condition has prevalence {prev:sig3}. A test has sensitivity {sens} and specificity {spec:sig3}.
Find the probability of a positive result (5 decimals) and the probability that a person
who tests positive has the condition (4 decimals).
drills.solution:
False-positive rate $= 1 - {spec:sig3} = {fp:sig3}$.
$P(+) = P(D)P(+ \mid D) + P(D^c)P(+ \mid D^c) = {prev:sig3}({sens}) + {q:sig4}({fp:sig3}) =$ **{pos:dp5}**.
Bayes: $P(D \mid +) = \dfrac{{tp:dp5}}{{pos:dp5}} \approx$ **{ppv:num4}**.

drills.title: Reliability of a series–parallel system
drills.prompt:
A signal passes through component $A$ (reliability {pa}), then through either of two
redundant units $B$ ({pb}) or $C$ ({pc}) in parallel, then through $D$ ({pd}). Components
fail independently. Find the system reliability (4 decimals).
drills.solution:
The parallel block fails only if both units fail: $R_{BC} = 1 - ({qb})({qc}) = {rbc:num4}$.
The system is $A$, the block and $D$ in series: $R = {pa} \times {rbc:num4} \times {pd} \approx$ **{rel:num4}**.

drills.title: At least one success in independent trials
drills.prompt:
Each independent attempt succeeds with probability {p}. (a) Find the probability of at least
one success in {n} attempts (4 decimals). (b) What is the smallest number of attempts that
makes the probability of at least one success at least {q}?
drills.solution:
(a) All fail with probability $({p1})^{{n}}$, so $P = 1 - ({p1})^{{n}} \approx$ **{pr:num4}**.

(b) Need $({p1})^n \le {qq}$. Taking logs (and flipping the inequality, since
$\ln {p1} < 0$): $n \ge \dfrac{\ln {qq}}{\ln {p1}} \approx {raw:num2}$, so $n =$ **{nmin}**.

drills.title: Mean, variance and cdf from a pmf table
drills.prompt:
A random variable $X$ has this pmf:

| $x$ | {v1} | {v2} | {v3} | {v4} |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $p(x)$ | {p1} | {p2} | {p3} | {p4} |

Find $E(X)$, $\operatorname{Var}(X)$ and the cdf value $F({v2})$. (4 decimals where needed.)

drills.title: Variance and linear functions of a random variable
drills.prompt:
A random variable $X$ has $E(X) = {mu}$ and $E(X^2) = {ex2}$. Let $Y = {a}X {b:signed}$.
Find $\operatorname{Var}(X)$, $E(Y)$ and the standard deviation of $Y$.
drills.solution:
Computing formula: $\operatorname{Var}(X) = E(X^2) - [E(X)]^2 = {ex2} - ({mu})^2 =$ **{var}**, so $\sigma_X = {sd}$.

Linearity: $E(Y) = {a}({mu}) {b:signed} =$ **{my}**.

The shift does not affect spread and the scale multiplies it by $|{a}|$:
$\operatorname{Var}(Y) = ({a})^2({var}) = {vy}$, so $\operatorname{SD}(Y) =$ **{sy}**.

drills.title: Normalizing a pmf and using LOTUS
drills.prompt: $X$ has pmf $p(x) = c\,x$ for $x = 1, 2, \ldots, {n}$. Find $c$, $E(X)$ and $E(1/X)$ as exact fractions.
drills.solution:
The probabilities sum to 1: $c(1 + 2 + \cdots + {n}) = {s}c = 1$, so $c =$ **{c:frac}**.

$E(X) = \sum x \cdot c\,x = c\sum x^2 = \dfrac{{s2}}{{s}} =$ **{mu:frac}**.

LOTUS with $g(x) = 1/x$: $E(1/X) = \sum \dfrac{1}{x}\cdot c\,x = {n}c = \dfrac{{n}}{{s}} =$ **{einv:frac}**.
Note that this is not $1/E(X)$.

drills.title: Binomial probabilities and moments
drills.prompt:
$X \sim \text{Bin}({n}, {p})$. Find $P(X = {k})$, $P(X \ge {k})$ (4 decimals) and the standard
deviation of $X$ (3 decimals).
drills.solution:
$P(X = {k}) = \binom{{n}}{{k}}({p})^{{k}}({q})^{{nk}} = {cnk:dp0}({p})^{{k}}({q})^{{nk}} \approx$ **{pk:num4}**.

"At least {k}" is the complement of "at most {km}": $P(X \ge {k}) = 1 - P(X \le {km}) \approx$ **{pge:num4}**.

$\sigma = \sqrt{np(1-p)} = \sqrt{{n}({p})({q})} \approx$ **{sd:dp3}** (the mean is $np = {mu:num2}$).

drills.title: Hypergeometric probabilities and moments
drills.prompt:
A lot of {nn} items contains {kk} defective ones. A sample of {n} is drawn without replacement.
Let $X$ be the number of defectives in the sample. Find $P(X = {k})$, $E(X)$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X)$
(4 decimals).
drills.solution:
$P(X = {k}) = \dfrac{\binom{{kk}}{{k}}\binom{{ng}}{{nk}}}{\binom{{nn}}{{n}}} \approx$ **{pk:num4}**.

$E(X) = n\dfrac{K}{N} = {n} \cdot \dfrac{{kk}}{{nn}} \approx$ **{mu:num4}**.

$\operatorname{Var}(X) = n\dfrac{K}{N}\left(1 - \dfrac{K}{N}\right)\dfrac{N - n}{N - 1}$, with correction factor $\dfrac{{nn} - {n}}{{nn} - 1} \approx {fpc:num4}$: $\operatorname{Var}(X) \approx$ **{var:num4}**.

drills.title: Geometric waiting times
drills.prompt:
Independent trials each succeed with probability {p}. Let $X$ be the number of trials until
the first success. Find $P(X = {k})$ and $P(X > {m})$ (4 decimals), and $E(X)$ and $\operatorname{SD}(X)$ (3 decimals).
drills.solution:
$k - 1 = {k1}$ failures, then a success: $P(X = {k}) = ({q})^{{k1}}({p}) \approx$ **{pk:num4}**.

More than {m} trials means the first {m} all fail: $P(X > {m}) = ({q})^{{m}} \approx$ **{pm:num4}**.

$E(X) = 1/p =$ **{mu:dp3}** and $\operatorname{SD}(X) = \sqrt{\,q}/p = \sqrt{{q}}/{p} \approx$ **{sd:dp3}**.

drills.title: Negative binomial probabilities
drills.prompt:
Each tested part passes with probability {p}, independently. Parts are tested until {r} have
passed; let $X$ be the number tested. Find $P(X = {k})$ (4 decimals), $E(X)$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X)$ (3 decimals).
drills.solution:
Part {k} must pass, and exactly {r1} of the first {k1} must pass:
$P(X = {k}) = \binom{{k1}}{{r1}}({p})^{{r}}({q})^{{kr}} = {cc:dp0}({p})^{{r}}({q})^{{kr}} \approx$ **{pk:num4}**.

$X$ is a sum of {r} independent geometric waits: $E(X) = r/p =$ **{mu:dp3}** and
$\operatorname{Var}(X) = rq/p^2 = {r}({q})/({p})^2 =$ **{var:dp3}**.

drills.title: Poisson probabilities
drills.prompt:
$X \sim \text{Poisson}({lam})$. Find $P(X = {k})$ and $P(X \ge {k})$ (4 decimals), and the standard
deviation of $X$ (3 decimals).
drills.solution:
$P(X = {k}) = e^{-{lam}}\dfrac{{lam}^{{k}}}{{k}!} \approx$ **{pk:num4}**.

$P(X \ge {k}) = 1 - P(X \le {km}) = 1 - \sum_{j=0}^{{km}} e^{-{lam}}\dfrac{{lam}^j}{j!} \approx$ **{pge:num4}**.

The variance equals the mean, {lam}, so $\sigma = \sqrt{{lam}} \approx$ **{sd:dp3}**.

drills.title: Poisson approximation to the binomial
drills.prompt:
$X \sim \text{Bin}({n:dp0}, {p:sig3})$. Find $P(X \le {k})$ exactly, and then using the Poisson approximation
(4 decimals each).
drills.solution:
Exact: $P(X \le {k}) = \sum_{j=0}^{{k}}\binom{{n:dp0}}{j}({p:sig3})^j(1 - {p:sig3})^{{n:dp0} - j} \approx$ **{exact:num4}**.

Approximation: $\lambda = np = {lam:num2}$, and
$P(X \le {k}) \approx \sum_{j=0}^{{k}} e^{-\lambda}\dfrac{\lambda^j}{j!} \approx$ **{approx:num4}**.
With $n$ large and $p$ small, the two agree closely.

drills.title: Counts in a Poisson process
drills.prompt:
Requests reach a server as a Poisson process with rate {rate} per hour. Let $N$ be the number of requests
in a period of {mins} minutes. Find $P(N = {k})$ and the probability of at least one request (4 decimals).
drills.solution:
The count in {mins} minutes is Poisson with mean $\lambda t = {rate} \times \tfrac{{mins}}{60} = {lam:num4}$.

$P(N = {k}) = e^{-{lam:num4}}\dfrac{({lam:num4})^{{k}}}{{k}!} \approx$ **{pk:num4}**.

$P(N \ge 1) = 1 - e^{-{lam:num4}} \approx$ **{p1:num4}**.

drills.title: Write an MGF and read off moments
drills.prompt:
$X$ takes the values 0, {a} and {b} with probabilities {p0}, {p1} and {p2}. Write the moment
generating function $M(t)$, and use it to find $E(X)$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X)$.

drills.title: Identify a distribution from its MGF
drills.prompt:
A random variable $Y$ has moment generating function
$$M_Y(t) = e^{{b:coef}t}\left({q} + {p}e^{{a:coef}t}\right)^{{n}}.$$
Recognize it as the MGF of $aX + b$ for a familiar $X$, and find $E(Y)$ and $\operatorname{Var}(Y)$.
drills.solution:
$M_{aX+b}(t) = e^{bt}M_X(at)$, and $({q} + {p}e^{t})^{{n}}$ is the MGF of $X \sim \text{Bin}({n}, {p})$.
So $Y = {a}X {b:signed}$ with $E(X) = {mx:num4}$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X) = {vx:num4}$.

$E(Y) = {a}({mx:num4}) {b:signed} =$ **{my:num4}** and $\operatorname{Var}(Y) = {a}^2({vx:num4}) =$ **{vy:num4}**.

drills.title: Sum of independent Poisson counts
drills.prompt:
Breakdowns on line A are Poisson({l1}) per week and on line B Poisson({l2}) per week, independently.
Let $T$ be the total number of breakdowns in a week. Find $P(T = {k})$ (4 decimals) and $\operatorname{Var}(T)$.
drills.solution:
$M_T(t) = e^{{l1}(e^t - 1)}e^{{l2}(e^t - 1)} = e^{{lam}(e^t - 1)}$, the MGF of Poisson({lam}).
By uniqueness $T \sim \text{Poisson}({lam})$, so
$P(T = {k}) = e^{-{lam}}\dfrac{{lam}^{{k}}}{{k}!} \approx$ **{pk:num4}**, and $\operatorname{Var}(T) =$ **{lam}**.

drills.title: Normalizing constant of a pdf
drills.prompt:
The pdf of $X$ is $f(x) = c\,x^{{pw}}$ for $0 \le x \le {bb}$ (0 elsewhere). Find $c$ and
$P(X < {aa})$. Exact fractions are fine; decimals to 4 places.
drills.solution:
Total area 1: $\int_0^{{bb}} c\,x^{{pw}}\,dx = c\cdot\dfrac{{bb}^{{p1}}}{{p1}} = 1$, so
$c = \dfrac{{p1}}{{bp}} \approx$ **{cc:num4}**. Then
$P(X < {aa}) = c\cdot\dfrac{({aa})^{{p1}}}{{p1}} = \left(\dfrac{{aa}}{{bb}}\right)^{{p1}} \approx$ **{pr:num4}**.

drills.title: Mean, variance and a probability from a pdf
drills.prompt:
$X$ has pdf $f(x) = \dfrac{12}{{b}^4}\,x({b} - x)^2$ for $0 \le x \le {b}$ (0 elsewhere). Find $E(X)$,
$\operatorname{Var}(X)$ and $P(X < {x0})$ (4 decimals).
drills.solution:
Expand $x({b} - x)^2 = {b}^2x - 2({b})x^2 + x^3$ and integrate term by term.

$E(X) = \dfrac{12}{{b}^4}\int_0^{{b}} x^2({b} - x)^2\,dx = \dfrac{12}{{b}^4}\cdot\dfrac{{b}^5}{30} = \dfrac{2({b})}{5} =$ **{mu:num4}**.

$E(X^2) = \dfrac{12}{{b}^4}\int_0^{{b}} x^3({b} - x)^2\,dx = \dfrac{12}{{b}^4}\cdot\dfrac{{b}^6}{60} = \dfrac{{b}^2}{5} = {ex2:num4}$, so
$\operatorname{Var}(X) = {ex2:num4} - ({mu:num4})^2 =$ **{var:num4}** (that is, ${b}^2/25$).

$P(X < {x0}) = \dfrac{12}{{b}^4}\int_0^{{x0}} x({b} - x)^2\,dx \approx$ **{pr:num4}**.

drills.title: Pareto cdf, quantiles and mean
drills.prompt:
A loss $X$ has cdf $F(x) = 1 - \left(\dfrac{{th}}{x}\right)^{{al}}$ for $x \ge {th}$ (and 0 below {th}). Find
$P(X > {x0})$ (4 decimals), the ${p}$-quantile of $X$, and $E(X)$ (3 decimals).
drills.solution:
$P(X > {x0}) = 1 - F({x0}) = \left(\dfrac{{th}}{{x0}}\right)^{{al}} \approx$ **{pr:num4}**.

Quantile: solve $1 - ({th}/x)^{{al}} = {p}$, so $({th}/x)^{{al}} = {q}$ and
$x = {th}\cdot({q})^{-1/{al}} \approx$ **{xp:dp3}**.

Mean by the tail formula: $E(X) = \int_0^{{th}} 1\,dx + \int_{{th}}^\infty \left(\dfrac{{th}}{x}\right)^{{al}}dx = {th} + \dfrac{{th}}{{am}} = \dfrac{{al}\cdot{th}}{{am}} \approx$ **{mu:dp3}**.

drills.title: Continuous uniform distribution
drills.prompt:
$X \sim \text{U}({lo}, {hi})$. Find $P({c1} < X < {c2})$ (4 decimals), the mean, and the standard deviation
of $X$ (3 decimals).
drills.solution:
The density is $1/{wid}$ on the interval, so $P = \dfrac{{c2} - {c1}}{{wid}} = \dfrac{{len}}{{wid}} \approx$ **{pr:num4}**.
$\mu = \dfrac{{lo} + {hi}}{2} =$ **{mu}** and $\sigma = \dfrac{b - a}{\sqrt{12}} = \dfrac{{wid}}{\sqrt{12}} \approx$ **{sd:dp3}**.

drills.title: Exponential probabilities and memorylessness
drills.solution:
Rate $\lambda = 1/{mean}$.

(a) $P(X \le {tt}) = 1 - e^{-{tt}/{mean}} \approx$ **{pr:num4}**.

(b) Memoryless: $P(X > {st} \mid X > {ss}) = P(X > {tt}) = e^{-{tt}/{mean}} \approx$ **{cond:num4}**.

(c) $1 - e^{-m/{mean}} = \tfrac12$ gives $m = {mean}\ln 2 \approx$ **{md:dp3}** months.

drills.title: Waiting times and counts in a Poisson process
drills.prompt:
Alerts arrive as a Poisson process at {rate} per hour. Find (a) the probability that the wait for the
next alert exceeds {tm} minutes (4 decimals), (b) the mean wait in minutes, and (c) the probability of
at least 2 alerts in a {hr}-hour period (4 decimals).
drills.solution:
(a) The wait $T$ is exponential with rate {rate} per hour; {tm} minutes is $\tfrac{{tm}}{60}$ hour, so
$P(T > \tfrac{{tm}}{60}) = e^{-{lt:num4}} \approx$ **{pw:num4}** (no alerts in that time).

(b) $E(T) = 1/\lambda = \tfrac{1}{{rate}}$ hour $=$ **{mw}** minutes.

(c) $N \sim \text{Poisson}({lh})$ in a {hr}-hour period: $P(N \ge 2) = 1 - e^{-{lh}}(1 + {lh}) \approx$ **{p2:num4}**.

drills.title: Normal probabilities
drills.prompt: $X \sim \text{N}({mu}, {sd}^2)$. Find $P({a} < X < {b})$ and $P(X > {c})$ (4 decimals).
drills.solution:
Standardize with $z = (x - {mu})/{sd}$: $z_a = {z1:num4}$, $z_b = {z2:num4}$, $z_c = {z3:num4}$.

$P({a} < X < {b}) = \Phi({z2:num4}) - \Phi({z1:num4}) \approx$ **{pab:num4}**.

$P(X > {c}) = 1 - \Phi({z3:num4}) \approx$ **{pc:num4}**.

drills.title: Normal percentiles
drills.prompt:
$X \sim \text{N}({mu}, {sd}^2)$. Find the value $x$ with $P(X \le x) = {p:sig4}$ (2 decimals), and the probability
that $X$ lies between {lo} and {hi} (4 decimals).
drills.solution:
$z = \Phi^{-1}({p:sig4}) \approx {zp:num4}$, so $x = {mu} + ({zp:num4})({sd}) \approx$ **{xp:num2}**.

{lo} and {hi} are ${k}$ standard deviations either side of the mean:
$P = \Phi({k}) - \Phi(-{k}) = 2\Phi({k}) - 1 \approx$ **{pin:num4}**.

drills.title: Normal approximation to the binomial
drills.prompt:
$X \sim \text{Bin}({n}, {p})$. Use the normal approximation with continuity correction to estimate
$P(X \le {k})$, then find the exact binomial value (4 decimals each).
drills.solution:
$\mu = np = {mu:num2}$ and $\sigma = \sqrt{np(1-p)} \approx {sd:num4}$. The bar for {k} ends at {kc}, so
$z = \dfrac{{kc} - {mu:num2}}{{sd:num4}} \approx {z:num4}$ and $P(X \le {k}) \approx \Phi({z:num4}) \approx$ **{approx:num4}**.

Exact: $\sum_{j=0}^{{k}}\binom{{n}}{j}({p})^j(1 - {p})^{{n} - j} \approx$ **{exact:num4}**.

drills.title: Integrals with the gamma function
drills.prompt: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^\infty x^{{m}}e^{-x/{sc}}\,dx$ (4 significant figures).
drills.solution:
Use $\int_0^\infty x^{\alpha - 1}e^{-x/\theta}\,dx = \Gamma(\alpha)\theta^{\alpha}$ with $\alpha - 1 = {m}$, so $\alpha = {al}$ and $\theta = {sc}$:
$$\Gamma({al})\,({sc})^{{al}} \approx {gal:sig4} \times {sc}^{{al}} \approx \mathbf{{val:sig4}}.$$
(Recall $\Gamma(n) = (n-1)!$ and $\Gamma(\tfrac12) = \sqrt\pi$, with $\Gamma(\alpha + 1) = \alpha\Gamma(\alpha)$.)

drills.title: Waiting time to the k-th event
drills.prompt:
Failures occur as a Poisson process with rate {rate} per day. Let $T$ be the time of failure number {k}.
Find $E(T)$ and $\operatorname{SD}(T)$ in days (3 decimals) and $P(T > {t})$ (4 decimals).
drills.solution:
$T$ is a sum of {k} independent exponential gaps, so $T \sim \text{Gamma}({k}, \theta)$ with scale $\theta = 1/{rate}$.
$E(T) = k\theta =$ **{mu:dp3}** and $\operatorname{SD}(T) = \sqrt{\,k}\,\theta =$ **{sd:dp3}**.

$T > {t}$ exactly when fewer than {k} failures occur by time {t}; that count is Poisson$({lt})$, so
$P(T > {t}) = \sum_{j=0}^{{km}} e^{-{lt}}\dfrac{{lt}^j}{j!} \approx$ **{pt:num4}**.

drills.title: Beta distribution moments and probabilities
drills.prompt: $X \sim \text{Beta}({a}, {b})$. Find $E(X)$, $\operatorname{Var}(X)$ and $P(X < {c})$ (4 decimals).
drills.solution:
Mean $= \dfrac{{a}}{{a} + {b}} = \dfrac{{a}}{{ab}} \approx$ **{mu:num4}**, and
variance $= \dfrac{{a} \cdot {b}}{({a} + {b})^2({a} + {b} + 1)} = \dfrac{{a} \cdot {b}}{{ab}^2 \cdot {ab1}} \approx$ **{var:num4}**.

The density is $\dfrac{x^{{a1}}(1 - x)^{{b1}}}{B({a}, {b})}$ with $\dfrac{1}{B({a}, {b})} = \dfrac{\Gamma({ab})}{\Gamma({a})\Gamma({b})} = {const}$, so
$P(X < {c}) = {const}\int_0^{{c}} x^{{a1}}(1 - x)^{{b1}}\,dx \approx$ **{pr:num4}**.

drills.title: The cdf method for a power of a uniform
drills.prompt:
$X \sim \text{U}(0, {b})$ and $Y = X^{{k}}$, which takes values in $(0, {bk})$. Use the cdf method to find
$P(Y \le {y0})$ and the density $f_Y({y0})$ (4 decimals).
drills.solution:
$F_Y(y) = P(X^{{k}} \le y) = P(X \le y^{1/{k}}) = \dfrac{y^{1/{k}}}{{b}}$ for $0 < y < {bk}$, so
$F_Y({y0}) = \dfrac{({y0})^{1/{k}}}{{b}} \approx$ **{cdf:num4}**.

Differentiate: $f_Y(y) = \dfrac{1}{{k}\cdot{b}}\,y^{1/{k} - 1}$, so $f_Y({y0}) \approx$ **{pdf:num4}**.

drills.title: Change of variables for a square root
drills.prompt:
$X$ is exponential with rate {lam}, and $Y = \sqrt{X}$. Use the change-of-variables formula to find the
pdf $f_Y(y)$ for $y > 0$, then compute $P(Y \le {y0})$ (4 decimals).
drills.solution:
$g(x) = \sqrt x$ is increasing on $x > 0$ with inverse $x = y^2$ and $\dfrac{dx}{dy} = 2y$. So
$$f_Y(y) = f_X(y^2)\cdot 2y = {lam:coef}e^{-{lam:coef}y^2}\cdot 2y = \mathbf{{two:coef}\,y\,e^{-{lam:coef}y^2}}, \quad y > 0.$$
Then $P(Y \le {y0}) = P(X \le {y0}^2) = 1 - e^{-{lam:coef}({y0})^2} \approx$ **{cy:num4}**.

drills.title: Inverse transform sampling
drills.prompt:
A lifetime has the Weibull cdf $F(x) = 1 - e^{-(x/{s})^{{k}}}$ for $x \ge 0$. A random number generator gives
$U = {u}$. Use inverse transform sampling, $X = F^{-1}(U)$, to produce a simulated lifetime (4 significant figures).

drills.title: Probabilities from a joint pmf table
drills.prompt:
An inspector records $X$, the number of worn brake pads on a bogie, and $Y$, an indicator of a
wheel flat. Their joint pmf is

$$\begin{array}{c|cc} & y = 0 & y = 1 \\ \hline x = 0 & {p00:num2} & {p01:num2} \\ x = 1 & {p10:num2} & {p11:num2} \\ x = 2 & {p20:num2} & {p21:num2} \end{array}$$

Find $P(Y = 1)$ and $P(X > Y)$.
drills.solution:
$P(Y = 1)$ is the marginal total of the $y = 1$ column: ${p01:num2} + {p11:num2} + {p21:num2} =$ **{py1:num2}**.

$X > Y$ holds in the cells $(1, 0)$, $(2, 0)$ and $(2, 1)$: ${p10:num2} + {p20:num2} + {p21:num2} =$ **{pgt:num2}**.

drills.title: Normalizing a joint density on a triangle
drills.prompt:
$(X, Y)$ has joint density $f(x, y) = c\,{pa}{pb}$ on the triangle $0 < y < x < 1$ (and 0 elsewhere).
Find the constant $c$, then find $P(X \le {hh})$ to 4 decimals.
drills.solution:
For fixed $x \in (0, 1)$, $y$ runs from 0 to $x$:
$\int_0^x {pa}{pb}\,dy = \dfrac{x^{{s1:int}}}{{b1:int}}$.
Then $\int_0^1 \dfrac{x^{{s1:int}}}{{b1:int}}\,dx = \dfrac{1}{{b1:int} \cdot {s2:int}}$, so $c = {b1:int} \cdot {s2:int} =$ **{cc:int}**.

The marginal of $X$ is $f_X(x) = c\,\dfrac{x^{{s1:int}}}{{b1:int}} = {s2:int}\,x^{{s1:int}}$ on $(0, 1)$, so
$P(X \le {hh}) = {hh}^{{s2:int}} =$ **{pr:num4}**.

drills.title: Conditional probabilities from a joint pmf
drills.prompt:
The joint pmf of $X$ and $Y$ is

$$\begin{array}{c|cc} & y = 0 & y = 1 \\ \hline x = 0 & {p00:num2} & {p01:num2} \\ x = 1 & {p10:num2} & {p11:num2} \\ x = 2 & {p20:num2} & {p21:num2} \end{array}$$

Find $P(Y = 1 \mid X = {kx})$ and $P(X = 2 \mid Y = 0)$, each to 4 decimals.
drills.solution:
Condition on the row $x = {kx}$, whose total is $P(X = {kx}) = {rowk:num2}$:
$P(Y = 1 \mid X = {kx}) = \dfrac{{cellk:num2}}{{rowk:num2}} =$ **{cy1:num4}**.

Condition on the column $y = 0$, whose total is $P(Y = 0) = {col0:num2}$:
$P(X = 2 \mid Y = 0) = \dfrac{{p20:num2}}{{col0:num2}} =$ **{cx2:num4}**.

drills.title: A conditional density on a triangle
drills.prompt:
$(X, Y)$ has joint density $f(x, y) = {cc:int}\,{pa}{pb}$ on $0 < y < x < 1$; its marginal is
$f_X(x) = {s2:int}x^{{s1:int}}$ on $(0, 1)$. Find the conditional density $f_{Y \mid X}(y \mid x)$ evaluated at
$y = {y0}$, $x = {x0}$, and find $P(Y \le {y0} \mid X = {x0})$. Give 4 decimals.
drills.solution:
Divide the joint density by the marginal:
$f_{Y \mid X}(y \mid x) = \dfrac{{cc:int}\,{pa}{pb}}{{s2:int}\,x^{{s1:int}}} = \dfrac{{b1:int}\,{pb}}{x^{{b1:int}}}$ for $0 < y < x$.
At $y = {y0}$, $x = {x0}$ this is **{dens:num4}**.

Integrate over $0 < y \le {y0}$:
$P(Y \le {y0} \mid X = {x0}) = \dfrac{{y0}^{{b1:int}}}{{x0}^{{b1:int}}} = \left(\dfrac{{y0}}{{x0}}\right)^{{b1:int}} =$ **{pr:num4}**.

drills.title: Racing independent exponentials
drills.prompt:
A pump's seal fails after an exponential time $X$ with mean {m1} years, and its bearing fails after
an independent exponential time $Y$ with mean {m2} years. Find $P(X < Y)$, the probability the seal
fails first, and $P(X > {ss},\ Y > {tt})$. Give 4 decimals.
drills.solution:
The rates are $a = 1/{m1}$ and $b = 1/{m2}$ per year. Integrating the product density over $x < y$ gives
$P(X < Y) = \dfrac{a}{a + b} = \dfrac{1/{m1}}{1/{m1} + 1/{m2}} =$ **{pfirst:num4}**.

By independence, $P(X > {ss},\ Y > {tt}) = P(X > {ss})\,P(Y > {tt}) = e^{-{ss}/{m1}}\,e^{-{tt}/{m2}} =$ **{pboth:num4}**.

drills.title: Covariance and correlation from a table
drills.prompt:
The joint pmf of $X$ and $Y$ is

$$\begin{array}{c|cc} & y = 0 & y = 1 \\ \hline x = 0 & {p00:num2} & {p01:num2} \\ x = 1 & {p10:num2} & {p11:num2} \\ x = 2 & {p20:num2} & {p21:num2} \end{array}$$

Find $\operatorname{Cov}(X, Y)$ (4 decimals) and the correlation $\rho$ (3 decimals).
drills.solution:
Marginals: $P(X = 1) = {px1:num2}$, $P(X = 2) = {px2:num2}$, $P(Y = 1) = {ey:num2}$.
$E[X] = {px1:num2} + 2({px2:num2}) = {ex:num4}$ and $E[Y] = {ey:num2}$.
$E[XY] = 1 \cdot {p11:num2} + 2 \cdot {p21:num2} = {exy:num4}$ (only cells with $x, y \ne 0$ count).
$\operatorname{Cov}(X, Y) = {exy:num4} - ({ex:num4})({ey:num2}) =$ **{cov:num4}**.

$E[X^2] = {px1:num2} + 4({px2:num2}) = {ex2:num4}$, so $\operatorname{Var}(X) = {ex2:num4} - {ex:num4}^2 = {vx:num4}$; $\operatorname{Var}(Y) = {ey:num2}(1 - {ey:num2}) = {vy:num4}$.
$\rho = \dfrac{{cov:num4}}{\sqrt{{vx:num4} \times {vy:num4}}} =$ **{rho:dp3}**.

drills.title: Covariance from a joint density
drills.prompt:
$(X, Y)$ has joint density $f(x, y) = {cc:int}\,{pa}{pb}$ on the triangle $0 < y < x < 1$. Find $E[X]$, $E[Y]$
and $\operatorname{Cov}(X, Y)$. Fractions are fine; decimals need 4 significant figures.
drills.solution:
For any powers, integrate $y$ from 0 to $x$, then $x$ from 0 to 1:
$E[X^pY^q] = {cc:int}\displaystyle\int_0^1\!\!\int_0^x x^{{pa:int} + p}y^{{pb:int} + q}\,dy\,dx = \dfrac{{cc:int}}{({pb:int} + q + 1)({s2:int} + p + q)}.$

- $E[X]$ ($p = 1, q = 0$): $\dfrac{{cc:int}}{{b1:int} \cdot {a3:int}} =$ **{ex:sig4}**.
- $E[Y]$ ($p = 0, q = 1$): $\dfrac{{cc:int}}{{b2:int} \cdot {a3:int}} =$ **{ey:sig4}**.
- $E[XY]$ ($p = q = 1$): $\dfrac{{cc:int}}{{b2:int} \cdot {a4:int}} = {exy:sig4}$.

$\operatorname{Cov}(X, Y) = E[XY] - E[X]E[Y] = {exy:sig4} - ({ex:sig4})({ey:sig4}) =$ **{cov:sig4}**.

drills.title: Variance of a linear combination
drills.prompt:
$X$ and $Y$ have standard deviations $\sigma_X = {sx}$ and $\sigma_Y = {sy}$ and correlation $\rho = {rho}$. Find
the variance and the standard deviation of $W = {aa:coef}X {bb:signedcoef}Y$. Give 2 decimals.
drills.solution:
$\operatorname{Cov}(X, Y) = \rho\sigma_X\sigma_Y = ({rho})({sx})({sy}) = {cov:num2}$. With $a = {aa}$, $b = {bb}$:
$\operatorname{Var}(W) = a^2\sigma_X^2 + b^2\sigma_Y^2 + 2ab\operatorname{Cov}(X, Y) = ({aa})^2({sx})^2 + ({bb})^2({sy})^2 + ({ab2})({cov:num2}) =$ **{vv:num2}**,
so $\operatorname{SD}(W) = \sqrt{{vv:num2}} =$ **{sd:num2}**.

drills.title: Sums and differences of independent normals
drills.prompt:
A freight run has two legs with independent normal times: leg 1 has mean {m1} min and SD {s1} min,
leg 2 has mean {m2} min and SD {s2} min. Find the probability that the total time exceeds {cut:int}
minutes, and the probability that leg 1 takes more than {dd} minutes longer than leg 2. Give 4
decimals.
drills.solution:
Both $X_1 + X_2$ and $X_1 - X_2$ are normal, and in both cases the variances add:
$\operatorname{Var} = {s1}^2 + {s2}^2 = {vt:int}$, SD $= {sdt:num4}$.

Total: mean ${m1} + {m2} = {mt:int}$, $z = \dfrac{{cut:int} - {mt:int}}{{sdt:num4}} = {z1:num2}$, so $P =$ **{p1:num4}**.

Difference: mean ${m1} - {m2} = {md:int}$, $z = \dfrac{{dd} - ({md:int})}{{sdt:num4}} = {z2:num2}$, so $P =$ **{p2:num4}**.

drills.title: Sum of independent Poisson counts
drills.prompt:
Line A has a Poisson number of signal faults per day with mean {l1}, and line B, independently, a
Poisson number with mean {l2}. Find the probability of exactly {kk} faults in total on a given day,
and of at most {kk}. Give 4 decimals.
drills.solution:
Independent Poisson counts add: $T \sim \text{Poisson}({l1} + {l2}) = \text{Poisson}({lt})$ (multiply the MGFs
$e^{\lambda(e^t - 1)}$).

$P(T = {kk}) = \dfrac{e^{-{lt}}\,{lt}^{{kk}}}{{kk}!} =$ **{pe:num4}**, and $P(T \le {kk}) = \sum_{j=0}^{{kk}} \dfrac{e^{-{lt}}{lt}^j}{j!} =$ **{pc:num4}**.

drills.title: Sum of two exponential stages
drills.prompt:
A repair has two independent stages, each taking an exponential time (in hours) with mean {mm}. Let $T$
be the total repair time in hours. Find $P(T > {tt})$. Give 4 decimals.
drills.solution:
Each stage has rate $\lambda = 1/{mm}$. By convolution, $T = X_1 + X_2$ has the gamma density (shape 2, scale {mm})
$f_T(z) = \lambda^2 z e^{-\lambda z}$ for $z > 0$. Integrating by parts,
$P(T > t) = \displaystyle\int_t^\infty \lambda^2 z e^{-\lambda z}\,dz = e^{-\lambda t}(1 + \lambda t).$
Here $\lambda t = {tt}/{mm} = {lt:num4}$, so $P(T > {tt}) = e^{-{lt:num4}}(1 + {lt:num4}) =$ **{pr:num4}**.
(The mean of $T$ is ${mean}$.)

drills.title: Mean and SD of a mixture
drills.prompt:
Brake blocks come from supplier A with probability {pa} (wear life mean {ma}, SD {sa}, in thousands of
km) or supplier B otherwise (mean {mb}, SD {sb}). A block is chosen at random. Find the mean and the
standard deviation of its wear life. Give 2 decimals.
drills.solution:
Law of total expectation: $E[Y] = {pa}({ma}) + {pb:num2}({mb}) =$ **{ey:num2}**.

Law of total variance:
within part $E[\operatorname{Var}(Y \mid X)] = {pa}({sa}^2) + {pb:num2}({sb}^2) = {within:num2}$;
between part $\operatorname{Var}(E[Y \mid X]) = {pa}({ma} - {ey:num2})^2 + {pb:num2}({mb} - {ey:num2})^2 = {between:num2}$.
$\operatorname{Var}(Y) = {vy:num2}$, so $\operatorname{SD}(Y) =$ **{sd:num2}**.

drills.title: Mean and SD of a random sum
drills.prompt:
The number of trains $N$ through a junction in an hour is Poisson with mean {lam}. Train loads are iid
with mean {mu} passengers and SD {sig}, independent of $N$. Find the mean and the standard deviation
of the total number of passengers $T$ in the hour (SD to 1 decimal).
drills.solution:
Condition on $N$: $E[T \mid N] = {mu}N$ and $\operatorname{Var}(T \mid N) = {sig}^2N$.

$E[T] = {mu}\,E[N] = {mu} \times {lam} =$ **{et:int}**.

$\operatorname{Var}(T) = \sigma^2E[N] + \mu^2\operatorname{Var}(N) = {sig}^2({lam}) + {mu}^2({lam}) = {vt:dp0}$ (a Poisson has $\operatorname{Var}N = E N$),
so $\operatorname{SD}(T) =$ **{sd:num1}**.

drills.title: A Poisson count with a random mean
drills.solution:
Given $X$, $E[Y \mid X] = X$ and $\operatorname{Var}(Y \mid X) = X$ (Poisson).

$E[Y] = E[X] = \dfrac{{lo} + {hi:int}}{2} =$ **{ey:num2}**.

$\operatorname{Var}(Y) = E[\operatorname{Var}(Y \mid X)] + \operatorname{Var}(E[Y \mid X]) = E[X] + \operatorname{Var}(X) = {ey:num2} + \dfrac{{wd}^2}{12} = {ey:num2} + {vx:num4} =$ **{vy:num2}**.

drills.title: Conditional distribution in a bivariate normal
drills.prompt:
Midterm ($X$) and final ($Y$) scores are bivariate normal with $\mu_X = {mx}$, $\sigma_X = {sx}$, $\mu_Y = {my}$,
$\sigma_Y = {sy}$ and $\rho = {rho}$. A student scored $X = {xx:num1}$ on the midterm. Find the conditional mean
and SD of her final score, and $P(Y > {cut:int} \mid X = {xx:num1})$. Give 2 decimals for the mean and
SD and 4 for the probability.
drills.solution:
$E[Y \mid X = x] = \mu_Y + \rho\dfrac{\sigma_Y}{\sigma_X}(x - \mu_X) = {my} + ({slope:num4})({xx:num1} - {mx}) =$ **{cm:num2}**.

$\operatorname{SD}(Y \mid X = x) = \sigma_Y\sqrt{1 - \rho^2} = {sy}\sqrt{1 - ({rho})^2} =$ **{csd:num2}**.

$z = \dfrac{{cut:int} - {cm:num2}}{{csd:num2}} = {zz:num2}$, so $P(Y > {cut:int} \mid X = {xx:num1}) =$ **{pr:num4}**.

drills.title: A sum of correlated normals
drills.prompt:
Delays (minutes) on two consecutive sections, $X$ and $Y$, are bivariate normal with means {mx} and {my},
SDs {sx} and {sy}, and correlation {rho}. Find the SD of the total delay $X + Y$ (2 decimals) and
$P(X + Y > {cut:int})$ (4 decimals).
drills.solution:
A linear combination of bivariate normal variables is normal. Its variance includes the covariance
term: $\operatorname{Var}(X + Y) = {sx}^2 + {sy}^2 + 2({rho})({sx})({sy}) = {vt:num2}$, so the SD is **{sdt:num2}**.
The mean is ${mx} + {my} = {mt:int}$.

$z = \dfrac{{cut:int} - {mt:int}}{{sdt:num2}} = {zz:num2}$, so $P(X + Y > {cut:int}) =$ **{pr:num4}**.

drills.title: Series and parallel lifetimes
drills.prompt:
A system has {nn} components with iid exponential lifetimes, each with mean {mm} hours. Find the mean
time to the *first* failure (2 decimals), and the probability that *all* components have failed by
{tt} hours (4 decimals).
drills.solution:
The first failure is the minimum: $P(X_{(1)} > x) = (e^{-x/{mm}})^{{nn}} = e^{-{nn}x/{mm}}$, an exponential with rate
${nn}/{mm}$, so its mean is ${mm}/{nn} =$ **{emin:num2}** hours.

All have failed by {tt} hours when the maximum is at most {tt}:
$P(X_{(n)} \le {tt}) = F({tt})^{{nn}} = \big(1 - e^{-{tt}/{mm}}\big)^{{nn}} =$ **{pmax:num4}**.

drills.title: Markov and Chebyshev bounds
drills.prompt:
A nonnegative repair time $X$ has mean {mu} minutes and standard deviation {sig} minutes; its
distribution is otherwise unknown. Find (a) the Chebyshev lower bound for $P({lo:num1} < X < {hi:num1})$
and (b) the Markov upper bound for $P(X \ge {cc:int})$. Give 4 decimals.
drills.solution:
(a) The interval is $\mu \pm k\sigma$ with $k = ({hi:num1} - {mu})/{sig} = {kk}$. Chebyshev:
$P(|X - \mu| \ge k\sigma) \le 1/k^2$, so $P({lo:num1} < X < {hi:num1}) \ge 1 - 1/{kk}^2 =$ **{cheb:num4}**.

(b) $X \ge 0$, so Markov applies: $P(X \ge {cc:int}) \le \dfrac{E[X]}{{cc:int}} = \dfrac{{mu}}{{cc:int}} =$ **{markov:num4}**.

drills.title: Sample size from Chebyshev and from the CLT
drills.prompt:
Measurements have standard deviation $\sigma = {sig}$. You want the sample mean to be within {eps} of
$\mu$ except with probability at most {dl}. Find the smallest $n$ that *guarantees* this by
Chebyshev's inequality, and the smallest $n$ that achieves it approximately by the CLT normal
approximation.
drills.solution:
Chebyshev: $P(|\bar X - \mu| \ge {eps}) \le \dfrac{\sigma^2}{n({eps})^2}$. Setting this $\le {dl}$ gives
$n \ge \dfrac{{sig}^2}{({eps})^2({dl})}$, so $n =$ **{ncheb:int}**.

CLT: $P(|\bar X - \mu| \ge {eps}) \approx 2P\Big(Z \ge \dfrac{{eps}\sqrt n}{{sig}}\Big)$. Setting $\dfrac{{eps}\sqrt n}{{sig}} = z = {zz:num4}$ gives
$n = \left(\dfrac{{zz:num4} \times {sig}}{{eps}}\right)^2$, rounded up: **{nclt:int}** (rounding $z$ differently can shift this by 1,
which is accepted). The guarantee costs many more observations than the approximation.

drills.title: CLT for a total of uniform amounts
drills.prompt:
A machine cuts {nn} lengths of cable, each independently uniform between {aa} and {bb:int} metres. Use the
Central Limit Theorem to approximate the probability that the total length exceeds {cut:int} metres. Give 4
decimals.
drills.solution:
Each length has mean $\dfrac{{aa} + {bb:int}}{2} = {mu:num2}$ and variance $\dfrac{({bb:int} - {aa})^2}{12} = {var1:num4}$.
The total of {nn} has mean ${nn} \times {mu:num2} = {mt:num2}$ and SD $\sqrt{{nn} \times {var1:num4}} = {sdt:num4}$, and is approximately normal.
$z = \dfrac{{cut:int} - {mt:num2}}{{sdt:num4}} = {zz:num2}$, so $P \approx$ **{pr:num4}**.

drills.title: Normal approximation to the binomial

calc.exact: if(side == 0, binomcdf(nn, pp, kc), 1 - binomcdf(nn, pp, kc - 1))

drills.prompt:
Each of {nn} passengers independently buys a reserved seat with probability {pp}. Use the normal
approximation with a continuity correction to estimate the probability that **{side} {kc:int}** buy one.
Give 4 decimals.
drills.solution:
$X \sim \text{Bin}({nn}, {pp})$ has mean $np = {mu:num2}$ and SD $\sqrt{np(1-p)} = {sd:num4}$.
The continuity correction treats {kc:int} as the interval from {kc:int} − 0.5 to {kc:int} + 0.5, so for "{side} {kc:int}" the
cutoff is ${edge:num1}$. $z = \dfrac{{edge:num1} - {mu:num2}}{{sd:num4}} = {zz:num2}$, giving **{pr:num4}**. (The exact binomial value is {exact:num4}.)

drills.title: CLT for a mean of Poisson counts
drills.prompt:
The number of faults per kilometre of track is Poisson with mean {lam}. Inspectors survey {nn} randomly chosen
kilometres. Approximate the probability that the average number of faults per kilometre exceeds {cut}.
Give 4 decimals.
drills.solution:
A Poisson count has mean and variance both equal to {lam}, so $\bar X$ has mean {lam} and SD
$\sqrt{{lam}/{nn}} = {se:num4}$. By the CLT, $\bar X$ is approximately normal:
$z = \dfrac{{cut} - {lam}}{{se:num4}} = {zz:num2}$, so $P(\bar X > {cut}) \approx$ **{pr:num4}**.

drills.title: Probabilities for the sample variance
drills.prompt:
A random sample of {nn} measurements is taken from a normal population with variance $\sigma^2 = {vv}$.
Find the probability that the sample variance $S^2$ is {side} {cut}. Give 4 decimals.

drills.title: A probability from the t distribution
drills.prompt:
A random sample of size {nn} is taken from a normal population with unknown mean and variance. Find
the probability that the sample mean exceeds the population mean by more than {kk} sample
standard deviations: $P(\bar X - \mu > {kk}S)$. Give 4 decimals.
drills.solution:
Divide both sides by $S/\sqrt n$: $\bar X - \mu > {kk}S \iff T = \dfrac{\bar X - \mu}{S/\sqrt{{nn}}} > {kk}\sqrt{{nn}} = {tt:num4}$.
For a normal sample $T \sim t_{{df}}$, so the probability is $P(t_{{df}} > {tt:num4}) =$ **{pr:num4}**.
(If $\sigma$ were known, the normal tail would give {pz:num4}; the $t$ tail is heavier.)

drills.title: Ratio of two sample variances
drills.prompt:
Independent random samples of sizes {n1} and {n2} are drawn from two normal populations with equal
variances. Find the probability that the first sample variance is more than {cc} times the
second: $P(S_1^2/S_2^2 > {cc})$. Give 4 decimals.
drills.solution:
$\dfrac{S_1^2/\sigma_1^2}{S_2^2/\sigma_2^2} \sim F_{n_1 - 1,\, n_2 - 1}$, and with $\sigma_1 = \sigma_2$ the ratio $S_1^2/S_2^2$ itself is
$F_{{d1},\,{d2}}$ (numerator df first). So $P(F_{{d1},{d2}} > {cc}) =$ **{pr:num4}**.

drills.title: Bias, variance and MSE of a shrinkage estimator
drills.prompt:
To estimate a mean $\mu$, an engineer combines the sample mean of $n = {nn}$ observations (population
SD $\sigma = {sig}$) with a prior guess of {m0}: $T = {ww}\bar X + {w1:num2}({m0})$. If the true mean is
$\mu = {mu}$, find the bias of $T$, its mean squared error, and the MSE of $\bar X$ for comparison.
Give 2 decimals.
drills.solution:
$E[T] = {ww}\mu + {w1:num2}({m0})$, so the bias is $E[T] - \mu = {w1:num2}({m0} - \mu) = {w1:num2}({m0} - {mu}) =$ **{bias:num2}**.
$\operatorname{Var}(T) = {ww}^2\,\dfrac{\sigma^2}{n} = {ww}^2 \times \dfrac{{sig}^2}{{nn}} = {var:num4}$.
$\operatorname{MSE}(T) = \operatorname{Var} + \operatorname{Bias}^2 = {var:num4} + ({bias:num2})^2 =$ **{mse:num2}**.

$\bar X$ is unbiased, so $\operatorname{MSE}(\bar X) = \sigma^2/n = {sig}^2/{nn} =$ **{msex:num2}**. Shrinking helps when the guess is close to
$\mu$ and hurts when it is far off.

drills.title: Comparing estimators of a uniform limit
drills.prompt:
A sample of $n = {nn}$ comes from Uniform$(0, \theta)$ with $\theta = {th}$. Two unbiased estimators are
$\hat\theta_1 = 2\bar X$ and $\hat\theta_2 = \tfrac{n+1}{n}X_{(n)}$. Find both variances and the efficiency of $\hat\theta_2$
relative to $\hat\theta_1$. Give 4 significant figures.
drills.solution:
$\operatorname{Var}(X) = \theta^2/12$, so $\operatorname{Var}(2\bar X) = 4 \cdot \dfrac{\theta^2}{12n} = \dfrac{\theta^2}{3n} = \dfrac{{th}^2}{3 \times {nn}} =$ **{v1:sig4}**.

From the density $nx^{n-1}/\theta^n$ of the maximum, $\operatorname{Var}(X_{(n)}) = \dfrac{n\theta^2}{(n+1)^2(n+2)}$, so
$\operatorname{Var}(\hat\theta_2) = \dfrac{(n+1)^2}{n^2}\operatorname{Var}(X_{(n)}) = \dfrac{\theta^2}{n(n+2)} = \dfrac{{th}^2}{{nn}({nn} + 2)} =$ **{v2:sig4}**.

Relative efficiency $= \dfrac{\operatorname{Var}(\hat\theta_1)}{\operatorname{Var}(\hat\theta_2)} = \dfrac{n + 2}{3} =$ **{eff:sig4}**.

drills.title: Fisher information and the Cramér–Rao bound
drills.prompt:
An iid sample of size {nn} comes from a **{fam}** distribution whose parameter (the success probability
for Bernoulli, the mean for Poisson) equals {par}. Find the Fisher information in one observation and
the Cramér–Rao lower bound for the variance of an unbiased estimator of the parameter. Give 4
significant figures.
drills.solution:
Use $I(\theta) = -E\big[\partial^2 \ln f(X; \theta)/\partial\theta^2\big]$.

- Bernoulli: $\ln f = x\ln p + (1 - x)\ln(1 - p)$, second derivative $-x/p^2 - (1-x)/(1-p)^2$, so $I(p) = \dfrac{1}{p(1-p)}$.
- Poisson: $\ln f = x\ln\lambda - \lambda - \ln x!$, second derivative $-x/\lambda^2$, so $I(\lambda) = \dfrac{1}{\lambda}$.

For this {fam} sample with parameter {par}: $I =$ **{info:sig4}**, and
$\text{CRLB} = \dfrac{1}{nI} = \dfrac{1}{{nn} \times {info:sig4}} =$ **{crlb:sig4}**. The sample mean attains it in both families.

drills.title: Exponential MLE and invariance
drills.prompt:
Six component lifetimes (hours) are {x1}, {x2}, {x3}, {x4}, {x5}, {x6}. Model them as iid exponential with
rate $\lambda$. Find the maximum likelihood estimate $\hat\lambda$ (4 significant figures) and the MLE of the
reliability $P(X > {tt})$ (4 decimals).
drills.solution:
$\ell(\lambda) = n\ln\lambda - \lambda\sum x_i$, and $\ell'(\lambda) = n/\lambda - \sum x_i = 0$ gives $\hat\lambda = n/\sum x_i = 1/\bar x$
($\ell''(\lambda) = -n/\lambda^2 < 0$, so it is a maximum). Here $\sum x_i = {tot:int}$, $\bar x = {xbar:num2}$, so
$\hat\lambda = 6/{tot:int} =$ **{lam:sig4}** per hour.

By invariance, the MLE of $P(X > {tt}) = e^{-{tt}\lambda}$ is $e^{-{tt}\hat\lambda} = e^{-{tt}/{xbar:num2}} =$ **{rel:num4}**.

drills.title: Normal MLEs from data

calc.mhat: mean(x1, x2, x3, x4, x5, x6)
calc.vhat: pvariance(x1, x2, x3, x4, x5, x6)
calc.s2: variance(x1, x2, x3, x4, x5, x6)

drills.prompt:
Gauge readings {x1:num1}, {x2:num1}, {x3:num1}, {x4:num1}, {x5:num1}, {x6:num1} are modeled as iid $N(\mu, \sigma^2)$ with both
parameters unknown. Find the maximum likelihood estimates $\hat\mu$ and $\hat\sigma$. Give 4 decimals.
drills.solution:
Setting the partial derivatives of $\ell(\mu, \sigma^2)$ to zero gives $\hat\mu = \bar x$ and $\hat\sigma^2 = \tfrac1n\sum(x_i - \bar x)^2$ (divide by $n$).

$\hat\mu = \bar x =$ **{mhat:num4}**. The squared deviations from $\bar x$ sum to ${ss6:num4}$, so
$\hat\sigma^2 = {vhat:num4}$ and, by invariance, $\hat\sigma = \sqrt{{vhat:num4}} =$ **{shat:num4}**.
(The unbiased $s^2 = {s2:num4}$ divides by $n - 1 = 5$ instead.)

drills.title: Method of moments versus MLE for a uniform limit
drills.prompt:
Five readings {x1:num1}, {x2:num1}, {x3:num1}, {x4:num1}, {x5:num1} are modeled as iid Uniform$(0, \theta)$. Find the
method-of-moments estimate and the maximum likelihood estimate of $\theta$. Give 2 decimals.
drills.solution:
Method of moments: $E[X] = \theta/2$; set it equal to $\bar x = {xbar:num4}$, so $\tilde\theta = 2\bar x =$ **{mom:num2}**.

Maximum likelihood: $L(\theta) = \theta^{-5}$ when $\theta \ge \max x_i$ and 0 otherwise. It decreases for $\theta \ge \max x_i$, so
$\hat\theta = \max x_i =$ **{mle:num2}**. (If the MoM value is below the maximum it is impossible as a value of $\theta$; the
bias-corrected $\tfrac{6}{5}\max x_i = {unb:num2}$ is the unbiased estimator based on the maximum, which has a much smaller variance than $2\bar x$.)

drills.title: t confidence interval for a mean
drills.prompt:
A random sample of {nn} brake-pad tests from a normal population gives $\bar x = {xbar:num1}$ mm and
$s = {ss:num1}$ mm. Construct a {lev} confidence interval for the mean wear $\mu$. Give the endpoints to 2
decimals.
drills.solution:
The pivot $\dfrac{\bar X - \mu}{S/\sqrt n} \sim t_{{df}}$ gives $\bar x \pm t^*\,s/\sqrt n$ with $t^* = {tc:num4}$ ({lev}, {df} df).
$SE = {ss:num1}/\sqrt{{nn}} = {se:num4}$, margin $= {tc:num4} \times {se:num4} = {me:num4}$.
Interval: from **{lo:num2}** to **{hi:num2}**.

drills.title: Chi-square confidence interval for a variance
drills.prompt:
A sample of {nn} rail-gauge measurements from a normal population has standard deviation $s = {ss:num1}$ mm.
Construct a {lev} confidence interval for the population variance $\sigma^2$. Give the endpoints to 2 decimals.
drills.solution:
Pivot: $(n-1)S^2/\sigma^2 \sim \chi^2_{{df}}$. For {lev} confidence, the lower and upper quantiles are
$\chi^2_L = {qlo:num4}$ and $\chi^2_U = {qhi:num4}$. With $(n-1)s^2 = {df} \times {s2:num4} = {num:num4}$:
$$\frac{{num:num4}}{{qhi:num4}} \le \sigma^2 \le \frac{{num:num4}}{{qlo:num4}},$$
so the interval is from **{lo:num2}** to **{hi:num2}** mm². (For $\sigma$: {slo:num2} to {shi:num2} mm.)

drills.title: Pooled two-sample t interval
drills.prompt:
Brake pads from supplier A ($n_1 = {n1}$) last on average {m1:num1} thousand km with SD {s1:num1}; pads from
supplier B ($n_2 = {n2}$) average {m2:num1} with SD {s2:num1}. Assuming normal populations with equal
variances, construct a 95% confidence interval for $\mu_A - \mu_B$. Give the endpoints to 2 decimals.
drills.solution:
Pooled variance: $s_p^2 = \dfrac{({n1} - 1)({s1:num1})^2 + ({n2} - 1)({s2:num1})^2}{{df}} = {sp2:num4}$, so $s_p = {sp:num4}$.
$SE = s_p\sqrt{1/{n1} + 1/{n2}} = {se:num4}$, and $t_{0.025,\,{df}} = {tc:num4}$.
Interval: $({m1:num1} - {m2:num1}) \pm {tc:num4} \times {se:num4}$, from **{lo:num2}** to **{hi:num2}**.

drills.title: Beta–binomial updating
drills.prompt:
A new coupling passes a stress test with unknown probability $\theta$, which is given a Beta({aa}, {bb}) prior.
In {nn} independent tests, {xx:int} couplings pass. Find the parameters of the posterior beta distribution
and the posterior mean (4 decimals).
drills.solution:
Posterior ∝ likelihood × prior $= \theta^{{xx:int}}(1-\theta)^{{fail:int}} \cdot \theta^{{aa} - 1}(1-\theta)^{{bb} - 1}$, which is Beta$({aa} + {xx:int},\ {bb} + {fail:int})$:
$a =$ **{a2:int}**, $b =$ **{b2:int}**.

Posterior mean $= \dfrac{a}{a + b} = \dfrac{{a2:int}}{{a2:int} + {b2:int}} =$ **{pm:num4}**, a weighted average of the prior mean {pmean:num4}
and the sample proportion {ph:num4} with data weight $\dfrac{{nn}}{{aa} + {bb} + {nn}} = {wt:num4}$.

drills.title: Normal–normal posterior and credible interval
drills.prompt:
A sensor offset $\theta$ has prior $N({m0}, {t0}^2)$. Readings are $N(\theta, {sig}^2)$ with known SD {sig}, and $n = {nn}$
readings average $\bar x = {xbar:num1}$. Find the posterior mean, the posterior SD and a 95% credible
interval (use 1.96). Give 2 decimals.
drills.solution:
Precisions add: prior $1/{t0}^2 = {p0:num4}$, data $n/\sigma^2 = {nn}/{sig}^2 = {pd:num4}$, total ${pt:num4}$. So the posterior
variance is $1/{pt:num4} = {vn:num4}$ and the posterior SD is **{sdn:num2}**.

Posterior mean $= \dfrac{{p0:num4}({m0}) + {pd:num4}({xbar:num1})}{{pt:num4}} =$ **{mn:num2}**.

95% credible interval: ${mn:num2} \pm 1.96 \times {sdn:num2}$, from **{lo:num2}** to **{hi:num2}**.

drills.title: Gamma–Poisson updating
drills.prompt:
A fault rate $\lambda$ (faults per day) has a gamma prior with shape {al} and rate {be} (scale $1/{be}$). Daily fault counts,
modeled as iid Poisson($\lambda$), are {c1}, {c2}, {c3}, {c4}, {c5}. Find the posterior shape and rate, and the
posterior mean (4 decimals).
drills.solution:
Likelihood ∝ $\lambda^{\sum x_i}e^{-n\lambda} = \lambda^{{tot:int}}e^{-5\lambda}$; prior ∝ $\lambda^{{al} - 1}e^{-{be}\lambda}$. The product is
$\lambda^{{al} + {tot:int} - 1}e^{-({be} + 5)\lambda}$, a gamma with shape **{a2:int}** and rate **{b2:int}**.

Posterior mean $= {a2:int}/{b2:int} =$ **{pm:num4}** (posterior SD $\sqrt{{a2:int}}/{b2:int} = {psd:num4}$), between the prior mean
${al}/{be}$ and the sample mean {xbar:num2}.

drills.title: Size and power of a binomial test
drills.prompt:
$X \sim \text{Bin}({nn}, p)$. To test $H_0: p \le {p0}$ against $H_1: p > {p0}$, you reject $H_0$
when $X \ge {cc}$. Find the size of the test and its power at $p = {p1}$ (4 decimals each).
drills.solution:
The power function $\pi(p) = P_p(X \ge {cc})$ increases in $p$, so the size is its value at the
boundary $p = {p0}$: $1 - P(X \le {cm1} \mid p = {p0}) =$ **{size:num4}**.

At $p = {p1}$: $\pi({p1}) = 1 - P(X \le {cm1} \mid p = {p1}) =$ **{pw:num4}** (so $\beta = {beta:num4}$).

drills.title: Power of a two-sided z test
drills.prompt:
$X_1, \dots, X_{{nn}}$ are $N(\mu, {sig}^2)$. A two-sided test of $H_0: \mu = {mu0}$ at
$\alpha = {al}$ rejects when $\bar X$ falls outside an interval $(c_1, c_2)$ centered at {mu0}.
Find $c_1$ and $c_2$ (2 decimals) and the power when $\mu = {mua:num1}$ (4 decimals).
drills.solution:
$\sigma/\sqrt n = {sig}/\sqrt{{nn}} = {se:num4}$ and $z_{\alpha/2} = {zs:dp3}$, so
$c_1 = {mu0} - {zs:dp3}({se:num4}) =$ **{lo:num2}** and $c_2 =$ **{hi:num2}**.

If $\mu = {mua:num1}$, then $\bar X \sim N({mua:num1}, {se:num4}^2)$ and the power is
$P(\bar X \le c_1) + P(\bar X \ge c_2) = \Phi({zlo:num2}) + 1 - \Phi({zhi:num2}) \approx$ **{pw:num4}**.

drills.title: Sample size for a one-sided z test
drills.prompt:
Measurements are normal with $\sigma = {sig}$. You will test $H_0: \mu = \mu_0$ against
$H_1: \mu > \mu_0$ at $\alpha = {al}$ and want power {pwr} when $\mu = \mu_0 + {delta}$.
What is the smallest sample size $n$ that achieves this?
drills.solution:
Power $1 - \beta$ at $\mu_0 + \delta$ needs $n \ge \left(\dfrac{(z_\alpha + z_\beta)\sigma}{\delta}\right)^2$ with
$z_\alpha = {za:dp3}$ and $z_\beta = {zb:dp3}$:
$\left(\dfrac{({za:dp3} + {zb:dp3})({sig})}{{delta}}\right)^2 = {nraw:num2}$. Round up: $n =$ **{nreq}**.

drills.title: Paired t test from data

calc.dbar: mean(d1, d2, d3, d4, d5, d6)
calc.sd: stdev(d1, d2, d3, d4, d5, d6)

drills.prompt:
Six units are each measured under treatment A and treatment B.

$$\begin{array}{c|cccccc} \text{unit} & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 & 6 \\ \hline A & {a1:num1} & {a2:num1} & {a3:num1} & {a4:num1} & {a5:num1} & {a6:num1} \\ B & {b1:num1} & {b2:num1} & {b3:num1} & {b4:num1} & {b5:num1} & {b6:num1} \end{array}$$

Test $H_0: \mu_D = 0$ against $H_1: \mu_D > 0$, where $D = A - B$. Find $\bar d$ (4 decimals),
the $t$ statistic (3 decimals) and the p-value (4 decimals).
drills.solution:
Differences $A - B$: {d1:num1}, {d2:num1}, {d3:num1}, {d4:num1}, {d5:num1}, {d6:num1}.
Their mean is $\bar d =$ **{dbar:num4}** and their s.d. is $s_d = {sd:num4}$.

$t = \dfrac{\bar d}{s_d/\sqrt 6} = \dfrac{{dbar:num4}}{{sd:num4}/\sqrt 6} =$ **{tt:dp3}** on 5 df, and the
p-value is $P(t_5 \ge {tt:dp3}) \approx$ **{pv:num4}**.

drills.title: Welch two-sample t test
drills.prompt:
Two independent normal samples give $\bar x_1 = {m1:num1}$, $s_1 = {s1:num1}$, $n_1 = {n1}$ and
$\bar x_2 = {m2:num1}$, $s_2 = {s2:num1}$, $n_2 = {n2}$. Using Welch's test of $H_0: \mu_1 = \mu_2$
against $H_1: \mu_1 \ne \mu_2$, find $t$ (3 decimals), the Satterthwaite degrees of freedom
(2 decimals) and the p-value (4 decimals).
drills.solution:
$s_1^2/n_1 = {v1:num4}$ and $s_2^2/n_2 = {v2:num4}$, so the standard error is
$\sqrt{{v1:num4} + {v2:num4}} = {se:num4}$ and $t = ({m1:num1} - {m2:num1})/{se:num4} =$ **{tt:dp3}**.

$\nu = \dfrac{({v1:num4} + {v2:num4})^2}{{v1:num4}^2/({n1} - 1) + {v2:num4}^2/({n2} - 1)} =$ **{nu:num2}**,
and the two-sided p-value is $2P(t_\nu \ge |t|) \approx$ **{pv:num4}**.

drills.title: Chi-square test for a variance
drills.prompt:
A normal sample of $n = {nn}$ has $s = {ss:num2}$. Test $H_0: \sigma = {sig0}$ against
$H_1: \sigma {side} {sig0}$. Find the test statistic (3 decimals) and the p-value (4 decimals).
drills.solution:
$\chi^2 = \dfrac{(n-1)s^2}{\sigma_0^2} = \dfrac{{dfree}({ss:num2})^2}{{sig0}^2} =$ **{chi:dp3}**, which has a
$\chi^2_{{dfree}}$ distribution under $H_0$. The alternative points to the tail where
$\sigma {side} {sig0}$, so the p-value is that tail area of $\chi^2_{{dfree}}$ beyond {chi:dp3}: **{pv:num4}**.

drills.title: Most powerful test for an exponential rate
drills.prompt:
$X_1, \dots, X_{{nn}}$ are exponential with rate $\lambda$ (density $\lambda e^{-\lambda x}$). The most
powerful level-{al} test of $H_0: \lambda = {l0}$ against $H_1: \lambda = {l1}$ rejects when
$\sum X_i \ge c$. Using $2\lambda\sum X_i \sim \chi^2_{2n}$, find $c$ (3 decimals) and the power of the
test (4 decimals).
drills.solution:
The ratio $L({l0})/L({l1}) = ({l0}/{l1})^{{nn}}e^{-({l0} - {l1})\sum x_i}$ decreases in $\sum x_i$, so reject for large $\sum x_i$.
Under $H_0$, $2({l0})\sum X_i \sim \chi^2_{{df2}}$, whose upper-{al} point is {q:dp3}. So
$c = {q:dp3}/(2 \cdot {l0}) =$ **{cc:dp3}**.

Under $H_1$, $2({l1})\sum X_i \sim \chi^2_{{df2}}$, so power $= P(\chi^2_{{df2}} \ge 2({l1})({cc:dp3})) = P(\chi^2_{{df2}} \ge {arg:dp3}) \approx$ **{pw:num4}**.

drills.title: Likelihood ratio test for a Poisson mean
drills.prompt:
Counts $X_1, \dots, X_{{nn}}$ are Poisson($\lambda$) with total $\sum x_i = {tot}$. Compute
$-2\ln\Lambda$ for the likelihood ratio test of $H_0: \lambda = {lam0}$ against $H_1: \lambda \ne {lam0}$
(3 decimals), and its approximate p-value from Wilks' theorem (4 decimals).
drills.solution:
The MLE is $\hat\lambda = \bar x = {tot}/{nn} = {xbar:num4}$, and
$-2\ln\Lambda = 2\left[\sum x_i\ln\dfrac{\bar x}{\lambda_0} - n(\bar x - \lambda_0)\right] = 2\left[{tot}\ln\dfrac{{xbar:num4}}{{lam0}} - ({tot} - {nn} \cdot {lam0})\right] =$ **{g2:dp3}**.

$H_0$ fixes one parameter, so compare with $\chi^2_1$: p-value $= P(\chi^2_1 \ge {g2:dp3}) \approx$ **{pv:num4}**.

drills.title: Likelihood ratio test for a proportion
drills.prompt:
In {nn} independent trials there are {xx} successes. Compute $-2\ln\Lambda$ for the likelihood ratio
test of $H_0: p = {p0}$ against $H_1: p \ne {p0}$ (3 decimals) and its approximate p-value (4 decimals).
drills.solution:
$\hat p = {phat:num4}$. With observed counts {xx} and {nmx} and null expected counts {e1:num2} and {e2:num2},
$-2\ln\Lambda = 2\left[{xx}\ln\dfrac{{xx}}{{e1:num2}} + {nmx}\ln\dfrac{{nmx}}{{e2:num2}}\right] =$ **{g2:dp3}**.

With 1 df: p-value $= P(\chi^2_1 \ge {g2:dp3}) \approx$ **{pv:num4}**.

drills.title: Two-proportion z test
drills.prompt:
Sample 1 has {x1} successes in {n1} trials; sample 2 has {x2} in {n2}. Test $H_0: p_1 = p_2$
against $H_1: p_1 \ne p_2$ with the pooled $z$ test. Find $z$ (3 decimals) and the p-value (4 decimals).
drills.solution:
$\hat p_1 = {ph1:num4}$, $\hat p_2 = {ph2:num4}$, pooled $\hat p = ({x1} + {x2})/({n1} + {n2}) = {pp:num4}$.
Standard error $\sqrt{\hat p(1 - \hat p)(1/{n1} + 1/{n2})} = {se:num4}$, so $z =$ **{zz:dp3}** and the
two-sided p-value is $2P(Z \ge |z|) \approx$ **{pv:num4}**.

drills.title: Chi-square goodness of fit
drills.prompt:
{nn} items fall into four categories with counts {o1}, {o2}, {o3}, {o4}. Test whether the category
probabilities are {q1}, {q2}, {q3}, {q4}. Find Pearson's $X^2$ (3 decimals) and the p-value (4 decimals).
drills.solution:
Expected counts: {ex1:num2}, {ex2:num2}, {ex3:num2}, {ex4:num2}. Contributions $(O - E)^2/E$:
{c1:num4}, {c2:num4}, {c3:num4}, {c4:num4}. Total $X^2 =$ **{x2:dp3}** on $4 - 1 = 3$ df, so the
p-value is $P(\chi^2_3 \ge {x2:dp3}) \approx$ **{pv:num4}**.

drills.title: Chi-square test of independence
drills.prompt:
Test whether the row and column variables are independent in this table of counts:

$$\begin{array}{c|ccc} & \text{C1} & \text{C2} & \text{C3} \\ \hline \text{R1} & {a1} & {a2} & {a3} \\ \text{R2} & {b1} & {b2} & {b3} \end{array}$$

Find the expected count for row R1, column C1 (2 decimals), $X^2$ (3 decimals) and the p-value (4 decimals).
drills.solution:
Row totals {ra} and {rb}, column totals {k1}, {k2}, {k3}, grand total {nt}.
$E_{11} = {ra} \cdot {k1}/{nt} =$ **{ea1:num2}**; the other expected counts are {ea2:num2}, {ea3:num2} (row R1)
and {eb1:num2}, {eb2:num2}, {eb3:num2} (row R2).

Summing $(O - E)^2/E$ over the six cells gives $X^2 =$ **{x2:dp3}** on $(2-1)(3-1) = 2$ df, so the
p-value is $P(\chi^2_2 \ge {x2:dp3}) \approx$ **{pv:num4}**.
